heraclea-pontica.t: Powerful Greek city on the southern Black Sea coast, known for its serf-like Mariandynian subjects, its philosopher-tyrants and its own daughter colonies.
heraclea-pontica.o: [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] was founded c. 560 BCE by settlers from [[s:megara|Megara]] joined by Boeotians, on the coast of north-west [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] where Heracles was said to have descended to the underworld. The colonists subdued the local Mariandynians, who became a dependent rural population compared by ancient writers to the helots of [[s:sparta|Sparta]].
heraclea-pontica.r: [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] controlled a wide territory, a strong fleet and trade in grain, [[e:timber|timber]] and nuts, and founded [[s:chersonesus-taurica|Chersonesus Taurica]] in [[e:crimea|Crimea]]. Its oligarchy gave way in 364 BCE to the tyranny of Clearchus, a former pupil of [[e:plato|Plato]] and Isocrates, and his family. His widowed daughter-in-law Amastris ruled and later married [[e:lysimachus|Lysimachus]]. The local historian Memnon preserved its story.
heraclea-pontica.e: After the tyranny ended, [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] regained independence, allied with [[e:rome|Rome]] and later with [[e:mithridates-vi-of-pontus|Mithridates VI of Pontus]]. In the [[e:third-mithridatic-war|Third Mithridatic War]] the Roman commander [[e:marcus-aurelius|Marcus Aurelius]] Cotta took and sacked it in 70 BCE. It recovered under Roman rule and survives as the Turkish town of Karadeniz Eregli.

hintata-emirate.t: The Masmuda Berber emirs of Marrakesh who ruled southern Morocco after the Marinid collapse, until the rising Saadis took their city.
hintata-emirate.o: The Hintata were a leading [[e:masmuda|Masmuda]] [[e:berbers|Berber]] tribe of the [[e:atlas-mountains|High Atlas]], prominent since [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] times. Under the [[s:marinid-sultanate|Marinid Sultanate]] their chiefs served as governors of [[e:marrakesh|Marrakesh]]. When Marinid authority collapsed in 1465 the Hintata [[e:emir|emirs]] became de facto independent rulers of the city and the Haouz plain.
hintata-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] governed a region of [[e:atlas-mountains|Atlas]] tribes and plains agriculture from the old imperial capital. They dealt with the Portuguese posts at Safi and Azemmour and are described by [[e:leo-africanus|Leo Africanus]], who visited in the early 16th century. Power rested on tribal alliances rather than a strong administration.
hintata-emirate.e: The [[s:saadi-sultanate|Saadi Sultanate]], rising in the Sous, pressed northward. The last important emir, [[e:muhammad-ibn-nasir-bu-shentuf|Muhammad ibn Nasir Bu Shentuf]], was assassinated in 1524, and the Saadis entered [[e:marrakesh|Marrakesh]] around 1525, making it their capital.

hokuzan.t: The northern kingdom of 14th-century Okinawa, centred on the great stone castle of Nakijin, conquered by Chuzan in 1416.
hokuzan.o: Hokuzan arose in the early 14th century in the mountainous north of Okinawa and the Motobu peninsula, one of three rival kingdoms that formed as local lords consolidated power. Its seat was Nakijin, whose long, winding stone walls survive as a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].
hokuzan.r: Hokuzan was the largest of the three kingdoms in area but the poorest in farmland. Its kings Haniji, Min and Hananchi sent tribute missions to [[e:ming-empire|Ming China]] from 1383, and the castle has yielded Chinese ceramics that show active trade. Power rested on alliances with local aji lords.
hokuzan.e: [[e:sho-hashi|Sho Hashi of Chuzan]] attacked Nakijin in 1416 with the help of disaffected Hokuzan lords; King Hananchi killed himself. [[s:chuzan|Chuzan]] then appointed a warden to govern the north.

hellenic-alliance.t: The alliance of Greek states, led by Sparta, that defeated the invasion of Xerxes at Salamis, Plataea and Mycale in 480-479 BCE.
hellenic-alliance.o: In autumn 481 BCE, as the Persian king [[e:xerxes-i|Xerxes]] gathered his army in [[e:asia-minor|Asia Minor]], delegates of the Greek states willing to resist met at the Isthmus of [[s:corinth|Corinth]]. They swore an alliance, ended their own feuds, including the war between [[s:athens|Athens]] and [[s:aegina|Aegina]], and sent envoys to seek help from [[s:argos|Argos]], [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]], [[s:corcyra|Corcyra]] and [[e:crete|Crete]], with little success.
hellenic-alliance.r: The alliance had a council of delegates (probouloi) meeting at the Isthmus, but command lay with [[s:sparta|Sparta]], which led on land and, through Eurybiades, at sea, although Themistocles' Athenian fleet was the largest. Some 31 states are named on the Serpent Column dedicated at [[s:delphi|Delphi]] after the war. Members who had sided with [[e:persia|Persia]] were threatened with punishment.
hellenic-alliance.e: After victories at Salamis (480 BCE) and [[s:plataea|Plataea]] and Mycale (479 BCE), the [[e:greeks|Greeks]] carried the war to the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. The arrogance of the Spartan regent Pausanias at [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] in 478 BCE led the Ionian allies to turn to [[s:athens|Athens]], which founded the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. The alliance itself lingered formally until 461 BCE.

hutsul-republic.t: A short-lived republic of Hutsul highlanders in the Carpathians, which declared for union with Ukraine after the fall of Austria-Hungary.
hutsul-republic.o: In November 1918, as Hungarian rule over Transcarpathia collapsed, a council of Hutsuls in the mountain village of Yasinia took power locally. In January 1919 it proclaimed its wish to join the [[s:ukrainian-peoples-republic|Ukrainian People's Republic]], with [[e:stepan-klochurak|Stepan Klochurak]] leading the local government.
hutsul-republic.r: The republic was a small highland territory of shepherds, woodcutters and rafters, run by an elected council and defended by a few hundred armed volunteers. It drove off Hungarian troops and tried to keep in contact with the [[s:west-ukrainian-peoples-republic|West Ukrainian People's Republic]] across the mountains, but it had little means of survival on its own.
hutsul-republic.e: In June 1919 Romanian troops occupied Yasinia and ended the republic. The Treaty of Saint-Germain then assigned Transcarpathia to [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]], and the region later formed [[s:carpatho-ukraine|Carpatho-Ukraine]]. The Hutsul Republic is remembered as an early expression of Ukrainian national feeling in Transcarpathia.

herakleopolitan-kingdom.t: The Ninth and Tenth Dynasties of Herakleopolis, which ruled northern Egypt in the First Intermediate Period and fought Thebes for the throne.
herakleopolitan-kingdom.o: Around 2160 BCE a family from Herakleopolis Magna, near the entrance to the Faiyum, took over the kingship from the [[s:eighth-dynasty-of-egypt|Eighth Dynasty of Egypt]]. Its founder, remembered as [[e:meryibre-khety|Meryibre Khety]] (Akhtoy), gave his name to the 'House of Khety', which held [[e:middle-egypt|Middle Egypt]] and the Delta.
herakleopolitan-kingdom.r: The Herakleopolitan kings depended on powerful provincial governors, notably the nomarchs of [[e:asyut|Asyut]], whose tomb inscriptions record the war against the south. The literary text known as the Teaching for Merikare, set in this period, gives advice on kingship, justice and defending the Delta frontier against Asiatics. Middle Egyptian literature, later regarded as classical, began to take shape in this age.
herakleopolitan-kingdom.e: From about 2130 BCE the kings fought the [[s:theban-eleventh-dynasty|Theban Eleventh Dynasty]] for control of Thinis and [[s:abydos|Abydos]]. Around 2025 BCE [[e:mentuhotep-ii|Mentuhotep II]] of [[s:thebes|Thebes]] took Herakleopolis and reunited [[e:egypt|Egypt]], opening the [[s:middle-kingdom-of-egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]].

habr-yunis-sultanate.t: A Somali sultanate of the Habr Yunis clan that broke away from the Isaaq Sultanate and played a part in the early Dervish movement.
habr-yunis-sultanate.o: The Habr Yunis, one of the [[s:isaaq-sultanate|Isaaq]] clans, set up their own sultanate around 1787, breaking away from the Isaaq Sultanate after a dispute over succession and authority. Its sultans were based near Toon and later in the area of Burao in northern [[s:somalia|Somalia]].
habr-yunis-sultanate.r: Like other [[e:somalis|Somali]] sultanates it was a clan polity, with the sultan presiding over elders and mediating conflicts according to customary and Islamic law. Its people herded [[e:camel|camels]] and traded through Berbera. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Nur Ahmed Aman was among the leaders who opposed British and missionary influence and joined [[e:mohammed-abdullah-hassan|Mohammed Abdullah Hassan]] in founding the [[s:dervish-state|Dervish movement]] in the 1890s.
habr-yunis-sultanate.e: The Habr Yunis signed protection treaties with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in the 1880s and became part of [[s:british-somaliland|British Somaliland]]. The sultanate's political role faded in the early 20th century, though the title survives as a traditional office.

hindu-shahis.t: The last Hindu dynasty of Kabul and Gandhara, which held the north-western gateway of India until Mahmud of Ghazni's invasions.
hindu-shahis.o: Around 822 Kallar, a [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] minister of the last [[s:turk-shahis|Turk Shahis]], overthrew his master and founded a new dynasty. The [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] Shahis ruled from [[e:kabul|Kabul]] and, after its loss to the [[s:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarids]] around 870, from Udabhandapura (Hund) on the [[e:indus|Indus]].
hindu-shahis.r: The Shahis ruled a [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Buddhist population from the [[e:kabul|Kabul]] valley to the [[e:punjab|Punjab]]. Their [[e:silver|silver]] 'bull and horseman' coins, showing Shiva's bull Nandi and a mounted warrior, were imitated widely across northern [[e:india|India]] and [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]]. They maintained alliances with [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]] and built temples in the Salt Range, and al-Biruni later praised their noble conduct.
hindu-shahis.e: The [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]] launched repeated invasions: Jayapala was defeated by Sabuktigin and then by [[e:mahmud-of-ghazni|Mahmud of Ghazni]] in 1001 at [[e:peshawar|Peshawar]], after which he committed suicide. His successors Anandapala and Trilochanapala lost further battles, and the dynasty ended by 1026 with the last Shahi kings in exile in [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]].

hammadid-emirate.t: A Berber dynasty of central Algeria whose fortified capital, the Qal'at Beni Hammad, is now a World Heritage site.
hammadid-emirate.o: [[e:hammad-ibn-buluggin|Hammad ibn Buluggin]], a son of the Zirid founder, governed the western lands of the [[s:zirid-emirate|Zirid emirate]] and founded the fortified city of Qal'at Beni Hammad in the Hodna mountains around 1007 to 1008. In 1015 he broke with his nephew, the Zirid emir Badis, and founded an independent dynasty.
hammadid-emirate.r: The Hammadid capital grew into a city of palaces, mosques and workshops, with a great minaret and fine glazed ceramics. The [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled the central [[e:maghreb|Maghreb]], drawing on [[e:sanhaja|Sanhaja Berber]] tribes. Pressure from the [[e:banu-hilal|Banu Hilal]] led al-Nasir ibn Alnas to build a new capital at Béjaïa (Bougie) on the coast in the 1060s, which became a busy port trading with Italian cities.
hammadid-emirate.e: In 1152 the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] under [[e:abd-al-mumin|Abd al-Mu'min]] took Béjaïa and the Qal'a, and the last emir, Yahya ibn [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]], surrendered. Béjaïa remained a centre of learning and trade, and the ruins of the Qal'a were listed as a World Heritage site in 1980.

hispania-ulterior.t: Rome's province of Further Spain, covering the rich south and west of Iberia from 197 BCE until Augustus split it into Baetica and Lusitania.
hispania-ulterior.o: After driving [[e:carthage|Carthage]] out of [[e:iberia|Iberia]] in 206 BCE, [[e:rome|Rome]] first governed the conquered south through commanders. In 197 BCE it created two provinces, each under a praetor; Hispania Ulterior covered the Guadalquivir valley and the lands to the west, including [[s:gadir|Gades]] and the former territory of the [[s:turdetani|Turdetani]].
hispania-ulterior.r: Governors based at Corduba, founded by [[e:marcus-claudius-marcellus|Marcus Claudius Marcellus]] in the 2nd century BCE, commanded armies and collected tribute from Iberian and Phoenician towns. [[e:silver|Silver]] mining, oil and grain made it rich, while campaigns against the [[s:lusitanians|Lusitanians]] dominated the 2nd century BCE. [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] served there as quaestor and then governor in 61 BCE.
hispania-ulterior.e: In the civil wars it was a stronghold of the Pompeians, defeated by Caesar at Munda in 45 BCE. From 27 BCE [[e:augustus-roman-emperor|Augustus]] reorganised it into [[s:hispania-baetica|Hispania Baetica]] and [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]], though the formal division took several years.

hiroshima-domain.t: A large domain on the Inland Sea, ruled by the Asano family from Hiroshima castle for two and a half centuries.
hiroshima-domain.o: When the Mori were reduced to [[e:choshu-domain|Choshu]] after [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]], [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave Aki and Bingo to [[e:fukushima-masanori|Fukushima Masanori]] in 1600. In 1619 the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] dismissed Masanori for repairing the flood-damaged castle without permission, and transferred [[e:asano-nagaakira|Asano Nagaakira]] to [[e:hiroshima|Hiroshima]] with about 426,000 koku.
hiroshima-domain.r: The Asano ruled the domain until its abolition. [[e:hiroshima|Hiroshima]], built on the delta of the Ota river, grew into a major castle town and port. The domain profited from [[e:rice|rice]], salt pans, oyster farming in Hiroshima Bay and paper, and controlled the shrine island of Itsukushima. The Shukkeien garden was laid out for Nagaakira from 1620.
hiroshima-domain.e: [[e:hiroshima|Hiroshima]] served as a base for the [[e:shogun|shogunate]]'s expeditions against neighbouring [[e:choshu-domain|Choshu]] in the 1860s but sought mediation and joined the imperial side in 1868. After abolition in 1871 it became Hiroshima Prefecture.

hispania-tarraconensis.t: The largest Roman province in Hispania, stretching from the Pyrenees to Galicia, governed from Tarraco for nearly five centuries.
hispania-tarraconensis.o: Tarraconensis was formed by Augustus from 27 BCE out of [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]], enlarged with the north-west after the [[e:cantabrian-wars|Cantabrian Wars]]. Augustus wintered at Tarraco in 26 to 25 BCE, and the city became the seat of the governor and of the imperial cult for the province.
hispania-tarraconensis.r: It was an imperial province under a senatorial legate, with the Legio VII Gemina based at León to guard the gold mines of the north-west. Tarraco had a great provincial forum and circus. The province contained hundreds of towns, from Caesaraugusta to Barcino, and exported wine, oil and minerals. Its legate [[e:galba|Galba]] was proclaimed emperor here in 68 CE. Under [[e:diocletian|Diocletian]] around 293 it was split into Tarraconensis, [[s:carthaginiensis|Carthaginiensis]] and [[s:gallaecia|Gallaecia]].
hispania-tarraconensis.e: The reduced province remained Roman longest in Hispania, despite Bagaudae revolts in the 5th century. Tarraco fell to the Visigothic king Euric in the early 470s, ending Roman rule in [[e:iberia|Iberia]].

histria.t: The oldest Greek colony on the western Black Sea coast, founded by Miletus near the mouth of the Danube.
histria.o: Milesian colonists founded Histria c. 657 BCE on a peninsula by the sea near the [[e:danube|Danube]] delta, in modern Dobruja, [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]]. It was named after the Istros, the Greek name for the Danube, and became the earliest Greek city on the western [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] coast.
histria.r: Histria traded [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], wine and pottery with the [[s:getae|Getae]] and [[e:scythians|Scythians]] for grain, fish, honey and slaves. [[e:aristotle|Aristotle]] mentions its shift from oligarchy to democracy. Its sanctuaries honoured [[e:zeus-polieus|Zeus Polieus]] and Aphrodite, and it struck [[e:silver|silver]] coins showing two heads and a sea eagle catching a dolphin.
histria.e: Histria was garrisoned by [[e:lysimachus|Lysimachus]] and revolted against him in 313 BCE. Its harbour silted up. In 72 to 71 BCE [[e:marcus-terentius-varro-lucullus|Marcus Lucullus]] brought the western Pontic cities under Roman control, and [[e:burebista|Burebista's]] [[s:getae|Getae]] sacked the city soon after. It revived under [[e:rome|Rome]] and was abandoned in the 7th century CE.

hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.t: The Caribbean islands owned by the Knights of Malta, a crusading order that briefly ran Saint Kitts, Saint Martin, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint Croix.
hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.o: [[e:phillippe-de-longvilliers-de-poincy|Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy]], a Knight of Malta and governor-general of the [[e:french-antilles|French Antilles]], persuaded the order to buy the French shares of [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Saint Kitts]], Saint Martin, [[s:saint-barthelemy-swedish|Saint-Barthélemy]] and [[e:saint-croix|Saint Croix]] from the bankrupt Compagnie des Îles d'Amérique. The purchase, approved by Grand Master Jean-Paul Lascaris-Castellar and [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]], was completed in 1651.
hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.r: Poincy governed the islands from his château near Basseterre on [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Saint Kitts]] as the order's lieutenant, while the French crown kept [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]]. It was the only overseas colony the Hospitallers ever held. The economy rested on tobacco and early [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], with enslaved Africans as labour. Saint-Barthélemy's settlement was destroyed by the Kalinago in 1656. After Poincy's death in 1660, [[e:charles-de-sales|Charles de Sales]] succeeded him.
hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.e: The venture never paid the distant order much. In 1665 the knights sold their rights to the new [[e:french-west-india-company|French West India Company]] of [[e:jean-baptiste-colbert|Jean-Baptiste Colbert]], returning the islands to ordinary French colonial rule. The episode left little trace beyond Poincy's buildings.

hierapytna.t: South Cretan port city that grew into the dominant power of eastern Crete in the Hellenistic age, destroying Praisos and contesting lands with Itanos.
hierapytna.o: Hierapytna lay at the narrowest point of eastern [[e:crete|Crete]], on the south coast at modern Ierapetra. Founded in the early [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]], it was a modest town in the Classical period and grew strong only in the Hellenistic age.
hierapytna.r: Hierapytna made treaties with [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] and with Hellenistic kings, supplying [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] and ships. It expanded aggressively, destroying [[s:praisos|Praisos]] c. 145 BCE and claiming the sanctuary of [[e:diktaean-zeus|Diktaean Zeus]] against [[s:itanos|Itanos]]. [[e:rome|Rome]] arbitrated the dispute in the late 2nd century BCE. The city was also accused of harbouring [[e:piracy|pirates]].
hierapytna.e: Hierapytna was among the last Cretan cities to fall to Metellus in 67 BCE. Rebuilt as a Roman port, it prospered with [[e:theatre|theatres]] and baths, and survives as the town of Ierapetra.

hirosaki-domain.t: The domain of the Tsugaru family at the northern tip of Honshu, founded by a vassal who broke away from the Nanbu.
hirosaki-domain.o: Oura Tamenobu, a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the Nanbu, seized the Tsugaru region in the 1570s and 1580s and won recognition directly from [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] in 1590, taking the name Tsugaru. His son Nobuhira completed Hirosaki castle in 1611.
hirosaki-domain.r: The breakaway left lasting enmity with the Nanbu of Morioka. The domain opened new [[e:rice|rice]] land, but its cold climate made harvests unreliable, and the Tenmei famine of the 1780s killed a large share of the population. The fourth lord, [[e:tsugaru-nobumasa|Tsugaru Nobumasa]], carried out reforms, and the domain later provided guards for Ezo against Russian incursions.
hirosaki-domain.e: In the [[e:boshin-war|Boshin War]] Hirosaki first joined the [[s:ouetsu-reppan-domei|Ouetsu Reppan Domei]] but switched to the imperial side in 1868. After the abolition of domains in 1871 it became part of Aomori Prefecture; Hirosaki castle's keep survives.

himyarite-kingdom.t: The last great kingdom of ancient Yemen, which unified south Arabia, adopted Judaism as a state faith and fell to Aksum in 525.
himyarite-kingdom.o: Himyar emerged in the highlands south of the [[s:kingdom-of-saba|Kingdom of Saba]]; its era, used for dating, began around 110 BCE. From the capital Zafar its kings, styled kings of Saba and [[e:dhu-raydan|Dhu Raydan]], fought Saba for centuries. [[e:shammar-yahrish|Shammar Yahrish]] absorbed Saba around 275 CE and the [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Kingdom of Hadramawt]] around 300, uniting all of south [[e:arabia|Arabia]].
himyarite-kingdom.r: Himyar controlled ports and the [[e:incense|incense]] lands and, under [[e:abikarib-asad|Abikarib As'ad]] in the 5th century, extended its authority into central [[e:arabia|Arabia]] through the [[s:kingdom-of-kinda|Kingdom of Kinda]]. Around 380 its rulers abandoned the old gods for a [[e:monotheism|monotheism]] close to [[e:judaism|Judaism]], and inscriptions to the Merciful replaced those to Almaqah. [[e:marib-dam|Marib Dam]] repairs and highland terracing sustained a dense agricultural population.
himyarite-kingdom.e: King Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar, known in Arab tradition as [[e:dhu-nuwas|Dhu Nuwas]], persecuted the [[e:massacre-of-najran|Christians of Najran]] in 523. In 525 the [[s:aksumite-empire|Aksumite Empire]] invaded under [[e:kaleb|Kaleb]], Yusuf was killed and [[s:aksumite-yemen|Aksumite Yemen]] took its place. Himyarite memory shaped later Yemeni identity and genealogy.

hapalla.t: Hapalla, one of the small Luwian vassal kingdoms created by the Hittites from the defeated land of Arzawa.
hapalla.o: Hapalla lay in western or south-western [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], on the eastern side of the [[s:arzawa|Arzawa]] lands, perhaps in later Pisidia. After [[e:mursili-ii|Mursili II]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] defeated Arzawa c. 1320 BCE, he made Targasnalli king of Hapalla.
hapalla.r: Known almost only from the treaty between [[e:mursili-ii|Mursili II]] and Targasnalli, which bound the king to send troops, return fugitives and remain loyal. Its people spoke Luwian.
hapalla.e: Hapalla stayed a Hittite [[e:vassal|vassal]] until the empire collapsed c. 1180 BCE, after which it disappears from the record.

hecatomnid-caria.t: Hecatomnid Caria, a Persian satrapy ruled as a dynastic kingdom by Mausolus and his family, whose tomb gave the world the word mausoleum.
hecatomnid-caria.o: Hecatomnus of Mylasa, a Carian noble, was made [[e:satrapy|satrap]] of Caria by the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] c. 395 BCE. He founded a dynasty that governed south-western [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] almost as independent kings while acknowledging Persian authority.
hecatomnid-caria.r: His son [[e:mausolus|Mausolus]] moved the capital to [[s:halicarnassus|Halicarnassus]], extended control over [[s:lycian-dynasts|Lycia]] and the islands, and combined Carian and Greek culture. After his death his sister-wife [[e:artemisia-ii-of-caria|Artemisia II]] completed his tomb, the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders. Siblings married each other and inherited power in turn, including Idrieus and Ada.
hecatomnid-caria.e: Pixodarus pushed his sister Ada aside, but in 334 BCE [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander]] of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] besieged [[s:halicarnassus|Halicarnassus]] and restored Ada, who adopted him as her son. Caria then passed to the Hellenistic kingdoms.

heraclea-lucania.t: Greek city founded jointly by Taras and Thurii in 433 BCE, seat of the Italiote League and site of Pyrrhus's first victory over Rome.
heraclea-lucania.o: After [[s:taras|Taras]] and [[s:thurii|Thurii]] fought over the territory of ruined [[s:siris|Siris]], they settled the dispute by founding a new city together in 433 or 432 BCE, with [[e:tarentum|Taras]] taking the lead. [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] was built on a plateau near the Siris and Aciris rivers, at modern Policoro.
heraclea-lucania.r: [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] was dominated by [[s:taras|Taras]], which moved the meeting place of the [[s:italiote-league|Italiote League]] there in the 4th century BCE, and it held the league's festival. The city prospered from farming the coastal plain. The bronze Tables of Heraclea, found in 1732, record on one side Greek temple land surveys and on the other a Roman municipal law of the 1st century BCE.
heraclea-lucania.e: In 280 BCE Pyrrhus defeated the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] under Laevinus at [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]], using elephants. In 278 BCE Heraclea made a treaty with [[e:rome|Rome]] on very favourable terms. It became a Roman municipium after the [[e:social-war-91-87-bce|Social War]] and declined in late antiquity.

huanca.t: A confederation of highland peoples in Peru's Mantaro valley who fought among themselves until conquered by the Incas, and later allied with the Spanish.
huanca.o: After the [[s:wari-empire|Wari Empire]] collapsed, the Mantaro valley in central [[e:peru|Peru]] was divided among the Huanca, or Wanka, and related groups such as the Xauxa. From about 1000 they formed communities of chiefdoms, and in the 14th century fortified hilltop towns such as Tunanmarca and Hatunmarca grew to house thousands.
huanca.r: The Huanca were divided into rival groups led by local war leaders called sinchis, and their hilltop towns reflect frequent warfare. They farmed [[e:potato|potatoes]] and other tubers, grew [[e:maize|maize]] in lower valleys and herded llamas. The valley was one of the most productive in the central [[s:andecavi|Andes]], and Hatun Xauxa later became a major [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] centre.
huanca.e: The [[e:inca-empire|Incas]] conquered the Huanca around 1460, resettling them in valley-floor villages. In 1533 Huanca lords allied with [[e:francisco-pizarro|Francisco Pizarro]] and supplied his troops; they later petitioned the Spanish crown for rewards. Jauja was briefly the Spanish capital in 1534.
huanca.re: Huanca religion, cult of Wari Willka

hotak-dynasty.t: A Ghilji Pashtun dynasty from Kandahar that threw off Safavid rule and, under Mahmud Hotak, captured Isfahan and toppled the Safavid dynasty in 1722.
hotak-dynasty.o: In 1709 [[e:mirwais-hotak|Mirwais Hotak]], a chief of the Ghilji Pashtuns, led a revolt in [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] against the Safavid governor Gurgin Khan, killed him and made Kandahar independent. He repelled Safavid attempts to retake the city and ruled until his death in 1715.
hotak-dynasty.r: Mirwais governed with the support of Pashtun tribal councils and avoided the title of king. His son [[e:mahmud-hotak|Mahmud Hotak]] invaded [[e:persia|Persia]], defeated the Safavid army at Gulnabad in 1722 and took [[e:isfahan|Isfahan]] after a long siege, forcing [[e:sultan-husayn|Shah Sultan Husayn]] to abdicate. Hotak rule in Persia was harsh and insecure, and Mahmud's successor Ashraf faced Ottoman and Russian advances as well as Safavid loyalists.
hotak-dynasty.e: [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]], fighting for the Safavid pretender [[e:tahmasp-ii|Tahmasp II]], defeated Ashraf at Damghan in 1729 and drove the [[e:afghans|Afghans]] out of [[e:persia|Persia]]. In 1738 Nader besieged and took [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] from Hussain Hotak, ending the dynasty. Its fall cleared the way for the later [[s:durrani-empire|Durrani Empire]].

hernici.t: Italic people of the Sacco valley in southern Latium, long-time allies of Rome whose towns are known for their massive polygonal walls.
hernici.o: The Hernici lived in the hills of the middle Sacco valley, between the [[e:latin|Latins]], the [[s:volsci|Volsci]] and the [[s:aequi|Aequi]]. Their name was explained from a Marsic word for rocks. They were an Italic people, probably related to the Sabellians, organised by the 5th century BCE in a league of towns centred on Anagnia.
hernici.r: Their towns, Anagnia, Ferentinum, Aletrium and Verulae, met in league councils at the Maritime Circus near Anagnia. Aletrium's acropolis with its huge polygonal walls is among the best preserved in [[e:italy|Italy]]. Wedged between the [[s:volsci|Volsci]] and [[s:aequi|Aequi]], the Hernici made a treaty with [[e:rome|Rome]] and the [[e:latins|Latins]], traditionally in 486 BCE, and fought alongside them for much of the 5th century.
hernici.e: Relations broke down in the 4th century. In 306 BCE Anagnia led a revolt and was punished with citizenship without the vote, while Ferentinum, Aletrium and Verulae, which stayed loyal, kept their independence as allies. All became Roman municipia after the [[e:social-war-91-87-bce|Social War]].

hocaba.t: A small Maya province of north-central Yucatán, one of the territories that emerged after the fall of Mayapan in the 1440s.
hocaba.o: Hocabá was one of the provinces (kuchkabalob) formed in northern Yucatán after the [[s:league-of-mayapan|League of Mayapan]] collapsed around 1441. It occupied a compact area south-east of present-day Mérida, between [[s:ceh-pech|Ceh Pech]], [[s:ah-kin-chel|Ah Kin Chel]] and [[s:sotuta|Sotuta]].
hocaba.r: The province was governed from the town of Hocabá by a ruler of the Iuit lineage, who held authority over the batabs, the heads of individual towns such as Homún. Like its neighbours, it lived from [[e:maize|maize]] farming, beekeeping and [[e:cotton|cotton]] weaving. It is known mainly from Spanish colonial records studied by Ralph Roys.
hocaba.e: Hocabá submitted to the Spanish in the early 1540s and was absorbed into the [[s:province-of-yucatan|Province of Yucatán]]. Its towns became colonial [[e:encomienda|encomiendas]].

herero-paramountcy.t: The cattle-rich Herero chieftaincy of Okahandja, whose 1904 rising against German rule ended in genocide.
herero-paramountcy.o: The Herero, [[e:bantu-peoples|Bantu-speaking]] [[e:cattle|cattle]] herders of central Namibia, had been raided for decades by [[e:jonker-afrikaner|Jonker Afrikaner's]] [[s:orlam-afrikaner-state|Orlam Afrikaner State]]. In 1863 they rose under Kamaherero, known as Maharero, at Otjimbingwe and won their independence, confirmed by the Peace of Okahandja in 1870.
herero-paramountcy.r: Maharero made Okahandja the seat of a paramountcy over many Herero chiefs, though authority was shared with lineage heads. Wealth lay in vast herds, and the holy fire of each homestead linked the living with ancestors. Rhenish missionaries were active, and in 1885 Maharero signed a protection treaty with [[e:germany|Germany]]; [[e:samuel-maharero|Samuel Maharero]] succeeded him in 1890.
herero-paramountcy.e: Land loss, debt and abuses under [[s:german-south-west-africa|German South West Africa]] led to the Herero rising in January 1904. After the battle of Waterberg, General von Trotha ordered their extermination; most Herero died in the Omaheke desert or in camps.

hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.t: The kingdom of the Hashemite dynasty east of the Jordan, which has survived regional wars and hosts millions of refugees.
hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised the independence of the [[s:emirate-of-transjordan|Emirate of Transjordan]] in 1946, and on 25 May the emir [[e:abdullah-i-of-jordan|Abdullah I]] became king; the country was renamed Jordan in 1949. In the 1948 war the Arab [[e:legion|Legion]] held the [[e:west-bank|West Bank]] and East [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]], which Jordan annexed in 1950.
hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.r: Jordan is a [[e:constitutional-monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] in which the king holds wide powers. [[e:abdullah-i-of-jordan|Abdullah I]] was assassinated in [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]] in 1951; after the brief reign of Talal, Hussein ruled from 1953 to 1999. Jordan lost the [[e:west-bank|West Bank]] to [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] in 1967 and expelled the Palestinian armed groups in the conflict of Black September in 1970. It has relied on foreign aid, [[e:phosphate|phosphates]] and remittances, and its population is largely of Palestinian origin.
hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.e: Hussein signed a peace treaty with [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] in 1994. His son [[e:abdullah-ii-of-jordan|Abdullah II]] succeeded him in 1999 and has kept the monarchy stable while hosting large numbers of Iraqi and Syrian refugees.

helian-xia.t: The Xiongnu kingdom of Helian Bobo, builder of the white-walled city of Tongwan on the edge of the Ordos desert, which briefly took Chang'an from the Jin.
helian-xia.o: Liu Bobo, of the Tiefu [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]], was a commander under [[s:later-qin|Later Qin]] who broke away in 407 and proclaimed himself Heavenly King of [[s:western-xia|Great Xia]], claiming descent from the ancient [[s:xia-dynasty|Xia dynasty]]. He later took the surname Helian.
helian-xia.r: Helian Bobo's mobile cavalry raided [[s:later-qin|Later Qin]] ruthlessly. Between 413 and 418 he built the capital Tongwan, its walls of pounded earth mixed with lime so hard that, it was said, builders were executed if an awl could pierce them; its white ruins survive in northern Shaanxi. In 418 he captured [[e:changan|Chang'an]] from the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]] forces left by [[e:emperor-wu-of-liu-song|Liu Yu]].
helian-xia.e: After Helian Bobo's death in 425, [[s:northern-wei|Northern Wei]] took Tongwan in 427 and captured [[e:helian-chang|Helian Chang]] the following year. His brother [[e:helian-ding|Helian Ding]] destroyed [[s:western-qin|Western Qin]] in 431 but was captured by the [[s:tuyuhun|Tuyuhun]] while crossing the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]] and handed to the Wei.

hsipaw-state.t: A northern Shan state on the Dokhtawady river whose last ruler, Sao Kya Seng, disappeared after the Burmese military coup of 1962.
hsipaw-state.o: Hsipaw, Shan [[e:thibaw-min|Thibaw]], was founded as a Shan principality in the Dokhtawady valley of the northern Shan plateau; tradition dates its ruling house to the 14th century. For long periods it was associated with the larger state of Onbaung, whose name it sometimes used.
hsipaw-state.r: The saopha of Hsipaw ruled from a haw, or palace, overseeing [[e:rice|rice]] and [[e:tea|tea]] growing and trade along the road from Mandalay to [[e:china|China]]. Hsipaw was a tributary of the Burmese crown and supplied consorts to the royal court. [[e:sao-hkun-hseng|Sao Hkun Hseng]], ruler from 1886, cooperated with the British and modernised his state.
hsipaw-state.e: Hsipaw became one of the British protected Shan states and joined the [[s:federated-shan-states|Federated Shan States]] in 1922. Its ruler surrendered powers in 1959. The last saopha, [[e:sao-kya-seng|Sao Kya Seng]], and his Austrian wife Inge Sargent, whose memoir told their story, were victims of the 1962 coup; he disappeared in army custody.

huron-confederacy.t: An alliance of Wendat nations between Lake Simcoe and Georgian Bay, the hub of the early French fur trade until Iroquois attacks dispersed it in 1649.
huron-confederacy.o: Wendat tradition holds that the Bear and Cord nations formed a league around 1440, joined by the Rock nation around 1590 and the Deer around 1610. Their country, Wendake or Huronia, lay in what is now Simcoe County, Ontario, where 20,000 to 30,000 people lived in palisaded villages of longhouses, among them Ossossane, the main town of the Bear.
huron-confederacy.r: A confederacy council of village and clan chiefs met to settle disputes and decide on war and trade, and the Feast of the Dead united communities through shared reburial of their dead. Women controlled fields of [[e:maize|maize]], beans and squash, whose surplus the Wendat traded north to Algonquian hunters for [[e:fur-trade|furs]]. Allied with [[s:new-france|New France]] from Champlain's visit in 1615, they hosted [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missions, including [[s:ile-sainte-marie|Sainte-Marie]] among the Hurons, founded in 1639.
huron-confederacy.e: Epidemics in the 1630s halved the population, and in 1648 to 1649 the [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]] destroyed the main towns and killed missionaries such as [[e:jean-de-brebeuf|Jean de Brébeuf]]. Survivors fled; some settled near [[s:province-of-quebec|Quebec]], where Wendake survives, and others joined the Petun to become the Wyandot.

hasanwayhid-dynasty.t: A Kurdish dynasty that ruled the western Zagros under Buyid overlordship and was praised for the security of its roads and its charity.
hasanwayhid-dynasty.o: [[e:hasanwayh-ibn-husayn|Hasanwayh ibn Husayn]], a chief of the Kurdish Barzikani tribe, took control of the mountains around Dinavar, [[e:hamadan|Hamadan]], Nahavand and Shahrizor in 959, as Buyid power was still being consolidated. His stronghold was the fortress of Sarmaj near Bisotun.
hasanwayhid-dynasty.r: Hasanwayh paid tribute to the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyid dynasty]] while ruling his tribal domains independently. His son [[e:badr-ibn-hasanwayh|Badr ibn Hasanwayh]] (979 to 1014), given the title [[e:nasir-al-dawla|Nasir al-Dawla]] by the [[e:caliphate|caliph]], became the most famous of the line. He was praised by chroniclers for building mosques and [[e:caravanserai|caravanserais]], protecting the pilgrim road and subsidising the poor and the holy cities, while keeping order among the Kurdish tribes.
hasanwayhid-dynasty.e: Badr was killed by his own troops in 1014. Shams al-Dawla, the Buyid ruler of [[e:hamadan|Hamadan]], and the [[s:kakuyid-dynasty|Kakuyid dynasty]] soon took over his territories, and the Hasanwayhids disappeared by 1015, partly replaced by the [[s:annazid-dynasty|Annazid dynasty]].

heungyo.t: A brief attempt to revive Balhae, proclaimed at Liaoyang in 1029 by a descendant of its founder in revolt against the Khitan Liao dynasty.
heungyo.o: In 1029 [[e:dae-yeon-rim|Dae Yeon-rim]], a descendant of Balhae's founder [[e:dae-joyeong|Dae Joyeong]] serving as an officer of the [[s:liao-dynasty|Liao dynasty]] at Dongjing, modern Liaoyang, rebelled against Khitan rule, killed local officials and proclaimed a new state called Heungyo, Xingliao in Chinese, with its own era name.
heungyo.r: The rebellion drew on [[s:balhae|Balhae]] descendants in the Liaodong region who resented Khitan taxes and labour demands. [[e:dae-yeon-rim|Dae Yeon-rim]] sent envoys to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] asking for help, but Goryeo declined to intervene.
heungyo.e: [[e:liao-dynasty|Liao]] armies besieged Dongjing, and in 1030 an officer opened the city gates; [[e:dae-yeon-rim|Dae Yeon-rim]] was captured and the state ended after about a year. Some of his followers fled to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]].

huastec-chiefdoms.t: The independent lordships of the Huastec (Teenek) people on the north-east Gulf Coast of Mexico, speakers of a Maya language long separated from the rest.
huastec-chiefdoms.o: The Huastec separated from other Maya speakers well over two thousand years ago and settled the lowlands of northern Veracruz, San Luis [[e:potosi|Potosí]] and Tamaulipas. From around 900 their region was organised into numerous small lordships centred on towns with circular platforms.
huastec-chiefdoms.r: Each lordship was led by its own chief, and there was no unified state. The Huastec were known for shell ornaments, distinctive black-on-white pottery and sculptures of youthful deities such as the Huastec Adolescent. The fertile Huasteca produced [[e:cotton|cotton]] and textiles. [[e:mexica|Mexica]] sources viewed them as foreign and depicted them with prejudice.
huastec-chiefdoms.e: From the 1450s the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] conquered much of the Huasteca and demanded tribute. [[e:hernan-cortes|Hernán Cortés]] subdued the region in 1522, and [[e:slave-raiding|slave raiding]] under [[e:nuno-de-guzman|Nuño de Guzmán]] devastated it. The Teenek people survive and their language is still spoken.

hedmark.t: Inland kingdom around Lake Mjøsa, one of the core lands of Halfdan the Black, where petty kings survived until Olaf Haraldsson.
hedmark.o: Hedmark, the farming land on the eastern shore of [[e:lake-mjosa|Lake Mjøsa]], was one of the richest districts of inland [[e:norway|Norway]]. The sagas say [[e:halfdan-the-black|Halfdan the Black of Vestfold]] gained it by war and inheritance in the 9th century, making it part of the base from which [[e:harald-fairhair|Harald Fairhair]] built his kingdom.
hedmark.r: Hedmark's wealth came from grain, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and iron from the surrounding forests. It shared the Eidsivating law assembly with the other Uppland districts. Local kings kept their position under the high kings, and the sagas name Hrørek as king of Hedmark in the early 11th century.
hedmark.e: Around 1018 [[e:olaf-ii-of-norway|Olaf Haraldsson]] crushed a revolt of the Uppland kings and had Hrørek blinded, ending the line of local kings. Hedmark became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]], and Hamar, on [[e:lake-mjosa|Lake Mjøsa]], became the seat of a [[e:bishop|bishop]] in 1152.

harfush-emirate.t: A Shia dynasty of emirs who governed Baalbek and the northern Beqaa Valley under the Ottomans for more than three centuries.
harfush-emirate.o: The Harfush were a [[e:twelver-shiism|Twelver Shia]] clan who held Baalbek and its district by the early Ottoman period. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], who conquered [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] in 1516, confirmed them as local governors and tax farmers, a role the family kept for generations.
harfush-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] collected taxes from the farmers of the Beqaa and passed revenue to the governors of [[e:damascus|Damascus]], keeping their own armed retainers. Their politics turned on rivalry and alliance with the Druze Ma'nids and later the Shihabis of the [[s:mount-lebanon-emirate|Mount Lebanon Emirate]]. [[e:yunus-al-harfush|Yunus al-Harfush]] allied with [[e:fakhr-al-din-ii|Fakhr al-Din II]] before falling out with him; he was executed in 1625. The family protected the [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] community of the Beqaa.
harfush-emirate.e: Internal feuds and conflict with the Shihabis weakened them in the 19th century. During the [[e:tanzimat|Tanzimat]] reforms the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] removed the last [[e:emir|emirs]] and exiled the family in the 1860s.

halogaland.t: The far northern chieftaincy of Viking Age Norway, home of the traveller Ohthere and of powerful lords who traded furs with the Sámi.
halogaland.o: Hålogaland stretched along the Norwegian coast north of [[s:earldom-of-lade|Trøndelag]], including the Lofoten islands. Its chieftains grew rich in the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]]: the great longhouse at Borg in Lofoten, over 80 metres long, was the seat of a local lord from the 6th century.
halogaland.r: The Hålogaland lords controlled trade in [[e:fur-trade|furs]], walrus [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], hides and dried fish, much of it taken as tribute from the Sámi. Around 890 Ohthere, a Hålogaland chieftain, described his life and his voyage round the North Cape to King [[e:alfred-the-great|Alfred of Wessex]], the earliest written account of the region. Power rested on chieftains rather than a formal kingdom.
halogaland.e: In the late 9th century the region came under [[e:harald-fairhair|Harald Fairhair]] and the earls of Lade, whose family is said to have come from Hålogaland. Local [[e:magnates|magnates]] such as Tore Hund remained powerful into the 11th century, before the area was fully integrated into the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]].

hungarian-tribal-federation.t: Confederation of seven Magyar tribes in the steppe of Etelköz, under Khazar overlordship, that set off to conquer the Carpathian basin in 895.
hungarian-tribal-federation.o: The Hungarians, Finno-Ugric speakers who had absorbed steppe Turkic culture, moved west and by about 830 lived in Etelköz, between the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]] and the lower [[e:danube|Danube]]. [[e:constantine-vii|Constantine VII]] describes seven tribes led first by Levedi, under the authority of the [[s:khazar-khaganate|Khazar Khaganate]].
hungarian-tribal-federation.r: They were mounted pastoralists and fearsome raiders, selling captives to traders on the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]]. Leadership was dual, with a sacral kende and a military gyula. Three Kabar tribes, rebels from the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]], joined them. They raided [[s:east-francia|East Francia]] from 862 and fought for [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] against [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] in 894. [[e:almos|Álmos]] and then his son [[e:arpad|Árpád]] were elected as leaders.
hungarian-tribal-federation.e: In 895 [[s:pechenegs|Pechenegs]] and Bulgarians attacked Etelköz, and the Hungarians crossed the Carpathians into the basin, founding the [[s:principality-of-hungary|Principality of Hungary]].

habbari-dynasty.t: An Arab dynasty that ruled lower Sindh from al-Mansura as nominal vassals of the Abbasids until Mahmud of Ghazni ended it.
habbari-dynasty.o: Sindh had been an Umayyad and then Abbasid province since the conquest by [[e:muhammad-ibn-qasim|Muhammad ibn Qasim]] in 711 to 712. As Abbasid control weakened, [[e:umar-ibn-abd-al-aziz-al-habbari|Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Habbari]], from an Arab family settled in Sindh, made himself ruler around 854 at al-Mansura, the provincial capital near modern Shahdadpur, while continuing to recognise the [[e:caliphate|caliph]].
habbari-dynasty.r: The Habbari [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled lower Sindh while the [[s:emirate-of-multan|Emirate of Multan]] held the north. Arab geographers such as al-Masudi and [[e:ibn-hawqal|Ibn Hawqal]] described al-Mansura as a prosperous city with a large mosque, where Arabic and Sindhi were spoken and trade passed between the [[e:indus|Indus]] and the [[e:persian-gulf|Persian Gulf]]. The ruling elite was [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] Muslim, while much of the population remained [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Buddhist.
habbari-dynasty.e: Around 1026 [[e:mahmud-of-ghazni|Mahmud of Ghazni]] attacked al-Mansura, reportedly because its ruler had adopted [[e:ismailism|Ismaili]] beliefs, and deposed the Habbari emir. Sindh came under the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavids]], and soon after the [[s:soomra-dynasty|Soomra dynasty]] rose to power.
