hispania-citerior.t: Rome's province of Nearer Spain, from the Ebro and the east coast into the Meseta, the base for Rome's long wars against the Celtiberians.
hispania-citerior.o: Hispania Citerior was created in 197 BCE as one of the two Roman provinces in [[e:iberia|Iberia]], covering the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] coast from the [[e:pyrenees|Pyrenees]] to beyond [[e:carthago-nova|Carthago Nova]]. It grew from [[e:rome|Rome's]] wartime base at Tarraco, established after [[e:gnaeus-cornelius-scipio-calvus|Gnaeus Scipio's]] landing in 218 BCE.
hispania-citerior.r: A praetor or consul governed from Tarraco or [[e:carthago-nova|Carthago Nova]], leading near-constant campaigns. Cato crushed the north-eastern revolt in 195 BCE, and [[e:tiberius-sempronius-gracchus-consul-177-bc|Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus]] made treaties with the [[s:celtiberians|Celtiberians]] in 179 BCE. The [[e:silver|silver]] mines around Carthago Nova were among the richest in the Roman world. The province steadily pushed inland, taking Numantia in 133 BCE.
hispania-citerior.e: It was the main [[e:theatre|theatre]] of Sertorius' war from 80 to 72 BCE, ended by [[e:pompey|Pompey]], and of Caesar's victory at Ilerda in 49 BCE. In 27 BCE [[e:augustus-roman-emperor|Augustus]] enlarged it as [[s:hispania-tarraconensis|Hispania Tarraconensis]], adding the north-west after the [[e:cantabrian-wars|Cantabrian Wars]].

hermunduri.t: A Germanic people of Thuringia and the upper Elbe, unusually friendly to Rome, who were allowed to trade freely inside the province of Raetia.
hermunduri.o: The Hermunduri were an [[e:elbe-germanic-peoples|Elbe Germanic]] people who, around 1 BCE, were resettled by the Roman commander Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus in lands vacated by the [[s:marcomanni|Marcomanni]] along the upper Main. Their territory came to stretch from the [[e:danube|Danube]] near Raetia north into Thuringia and the Saale region.
hermunduri.r: [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] calls them faithful to [[e:rome|Rome]] and notes that, alone among Germans, they could enter the colony of [[e:augsburg|Augusta Vindelicorum]] ([[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]]) without guard to trade. In 19 their leader Vibilius helped overthrow Catualda, and in 50 he also brought down Vannius. In 58 they defeated the [[s:chatti|Chatti]] in a war over sacred salt springs.
hermunduri.e: The Hermunduri took part in the [[e:marcomannic-wars|Marcomannic Wars]] against [[e:rome|Rome]] in the 160s and 170s. They disappear from sources in the 3rd century, and most historians see them as one of the roots of the later [[s:kingdom-of-the-thuringians|Thuringians]], whose name may derive from theirs.

hospitaller-rhodes.t: Rhodes under the Knights Hospitaller, a crusading order-state that held out against Mamluks and Ottomans for two centuries before Suleiman took it in 1522.
hospitaller-rhodes.o: After the fall of [[e:acre|Acre]] in 1291 the Knights of the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Order of Saint John]] moved to [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]]. Seeking a base of their own, Grand Master Foulques de Villaret attacked Byzantine [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] in 1306, and the city fell in 1309-1310. The order also took nearby islands and later built the castle of Saint Peter at [[s:halicarnassus|Bodrum]].
hospitaller-rhodes.r: The Grand Master and a council of knights, organised by national langues, governed a Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] population and [[e:latin|Latin]] settlers. The order ran a hospital, built great walls and the Palace of the Grand Master, and used its [[e:galley|galleys]] against Muslim shipping. It acquired much of the [[e:knights-templar|Templars]]' wealth after 1312. Under Pierre d'Aubusson it repulsed the Ottoman siege of 1480.
hospitaller-rhodes.e: In 1522 [[e:suleiman-the-magnificent|Suleiman the Magnificent]] besieged [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] with a vast army. After six months Grand Master Philippe Villiers de l'Isle-Adam surrendered on honourable terms, and the knights left in early 1523, settling in Malta in 1530. Their medieval city is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].

hasinai-confederacy.t: The Caddo confederacy of east Texas whose word for friend, taysha, gave the name Texas to a Spanish province and a modern state.
hasinai-confederacy.o: The Hasinai were one of three Caddo confederacies, alongside the Kadohadacho and Natchitoches, descended from mound-building Caddoan cultures that flourished from around 800 in the forests where Texas, [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]], Arkansas and Oklahoma meet. By about 1500 several Hasinai communities along the upper Neches and Angelina rivers had formed a loose alliance.
hasinai-confederacy.r: A religious leader, the xinesi, kept the sacred fire in a temple, while village chiefs, the caddi, governed with the help of officials. Dispersed farmsteads of tall grass houses grew [[e:maize|maize]], beans and squash, and the Caddo made fine engraved pottery and traded salt and bows. [[s:spanish-texas|Spanish Texas]] began with the mission of [[e:san-francisco|San Francisco]] de los Tejas among the Hasinai in 1690, and after 1714 they traded guns and horses with the French at Natchitoches.
hasinai-confederacy.e: Epidemics sharply reduced the Hasinai in the 18th century. After Texan independence they were pushed onto the Brazos Reserve in 1855 and in 1859 removed to [[e:indian-territory|Indian Territory]]. Their descendants form the Caddo Nation of Oklahoma.

hungary.t: Present-day Hungary, a parliamentary republic since 1989 and member of NATO and the European Union, long dominated by Viktor Orbán's Fidesz.
hungary.o: On 23 October 1989, the anniversary of the 1956 revolution, the Republic of Hungary was proclaimed, replacing the [[s:hungarian-peoples-republic|Hungarian People's Republic]] after [[e:hungarian-round-table-talks|Round Table]] talks between communists and opposition. The first free elections in spring 1990 brought József Antall's Hungarian Democratic Forum to power, and [[e:arpad-goncz|Árpád Göncz]] became president.
hungary.r: Hungary is a parliamentary republic with a prime minister responsible to a single-chamber [[e:national-assembly-of-hungary|National Assembly]]. The 1990s brought rapid privatisation and foreign investment, followed by alternating governments of left and right. Fidesz under [[e:viktor-orban|Viktor Orbán]] won a two-thirds majority in 2010 and adopted a new Fundamental Law in 2011, which renamed the state simply Hungary.
hungary.e: Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the [[e:european-union|European Union]] in 2004. Orbán's governments, re-elected in 2014, 2018 and 2022, have clashed with the EU over the [[e:rule-of-law|rule of law]], media freedom and migration, and some EU funds were withheld. In April 2026 Péter [[e:magyars|Magyar's]] Tisza party won a two-thirds majority, ending sixteen years of Fidesz government.

hellenic-state-1941-1944.t: Greece's collaborationist government during the Axis occupation, which ruled in Athens under German and Italian control during famine and resistance.
hellenic-state-1941-1944.o: After [[e:germany|Germany]] invaded [[e:greece|Greece]] in April 1941, General Georgios Tsolakoglou surrendered the army and was installed as prime minister of a collaborationist government in [[s:athens|Athens]], while King George II and the legitimate government fled to [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. The country was divided into German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation zones.
hellenic-state-1941-1944.r: The regime had little real authority. [[e:axis-powers|Axis]] requisitions and [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]] caused the great famine of 1941-1942, in which tens of thousands died in [[s:athens|Athens]]. Tsolakoglou was succeeded by [[e:konstantinos-logothetopoulos|Konstantinos Logothetopoulos]] and then [[e:ioannis-rallis|Ioannis Rallis]], who formed the Security Battalions to fight the communist-led resistance of EAM-ELAS. The [[e:jews|Jews]] of Thessaloniki were deported in 1943 with little resistance from the government.
hellenic-state-1941-1944.e: As German forces withdrew in October 1944, the government collapsed and the government-in-exile returned. Its leaders were tried as collaborators in 1945. The bitter divisions of the occupation fed directly into the Greek Civil War.

harjumaa.t: Inland county of northern Estonia that fell to Denmark in 1219 and later launched the great St George's Night Uprising of 1343.
harjumaa.o: Harjumaa, inland from the coast around modern [[s:reval|Tallinn]], was one of the ancient Estonian lands, made up of several parishes with hillforts. It was closely linked to the coastal county of [[s:ravala|Rävala]], and the two are often treated together in the sources.
harjumaa.r: Its elders led the free farmers in war and council. The district grew grain on limestone soils and traded through the harbour at Lindanise. [[e:henry-of-livonia|Henry of Livonia]] names Harjumaa's people among those who met for a common assembly at Raikküla.
harjumaa.e: After the Danish victory at Lindanise in 1219, Harjumaa passed under Danish rule and became part of the [[s:duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346|Duchy of Estonia]] (1219-1346). In 1343 its peasants began the [[e:st-georges-night-uprising|St George's Night Uprising]], which was crushed by the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], after which [[e:denmark|Denmark]] sold the duchy to the [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]].

hafsid-sultanate.t: The Berber dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya from Tunis for over three centuries, a Mediterranean trading power that claimed the Almohad caliphate's mantle.
hafsid-sultanate.o: The [[e:hafsid-dynasty|Hafsids]] descended from [[e:abu-hafs-umar-al-hintati|Abu Hafs Umar]], a companion of the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] founder [[e:ibn-tumart|Ibn Tumart]]. [[e:abu-muhammad-abd-al-wahid-ibn-abi-hafs|Abu Muhammad]], a son, governed [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]] for the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] from 1207. In 1229 his son [[e:abu-zakariya-yahya-i|Abu Zakariya Yahya]] broke with [[e:marrakesh|Marrakesh]], declaring independence at [[e:tunis|Tunis]] and extending his rule to Constantine, Bejaia and [[e:algiers|Algiers]].
hafsid-sultanate.r: [[e:al-mustansir-billah|Al-Mustansir]] took the title of [[e:caliphate|caliph]] in 1253 and was briefly recognised in [[e:mecca|Mecca]]; in 1270 he survived the [[e:crusade|crusade]] of [[e:louis-ix-of-france|Louis IX]], who died besieging [[e:tunis|Tunis]]. Tunis grew rich on treaties with [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]], [[e:venice|Venice]], Pisa and [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]], exporting grain, wool and leather. The Zaytuna mosque flourished, and Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332. Abu [[e:fari|Faris]] and Abu Amr Uthman restored strength in the 15th century.
hafsid-sultanate.e: In the 16th century [[e:tunis|Tunis]] was squeezed between [[s:habsburg-spain|Habsburg Spain]] and the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]]. [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] took the city in 1535 and propped up the [[e:hafsid-dynasty|Hafsids]] as [[e:vassal|vassals]], until Sinan Pasha's Ottoman conquest in 1574 ended the dynasty and created [[s:ottoman-tunisia|Ottoman Tunisia]].

herodian-kingdom-of-chalcis.t: A small Roman client kingdom in the Beqaa Valley given to members of the Herodian family, whose kings also controlled the Jerusalem high priesthood.
herodian-kingdom-of-chalcis.o: [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]], in the [[e:beqaa-valley|Beqaa Valley]], had been the seat of an [[s:ituraea|Ituraean principality]] under Ptolemy son of Mennaeus and Lysanias. In 41 Claudius gave it with the title king to Herod, brother of [[e:herod-agrippa-i|Agrippa I]], now known as [[e:herod-of-chalcis|Herod of Chalcis]].
herodian-kingdom-of-chalcis.r: [[e:herod-of-chalcis|Herod of Chalcis]] also received from Claudius authority over the [[e:temple-in-jerusalem|Temple in Jerusalem]] and the right to appoint high priests, an influence passed on to his successors. After his death in 48, [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]] went to his nephew [[e:agrippa-ii|Agrippa II]], who exchanged it in 53 for larger lands further south. Little is known of internal government; the population was mostly Ituraean Arab and Syrian, with Greek used in administration.
herodian-kingdom-of-chalcis.e: From 57 [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]] was ruled by Aristobulus, son of [[e:herod-of-chalcis|Herod of Chalcis]] and husband of Salome, who also held [[s:lesser-armenia|Lesser Armenia]]. After his reign the territory was annexed to the province of [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] around 92.

hungarian-soviet-republic.t: Communist regime of Béla Kun that ruled Hungary for 133 days in 1919, the second Soviet-style state in the world after Russia.
hungarian-soviet-republic.o: When the [[e:allies|Allies]]' Vix Note in March 1919 demanded further Hungarian withdrawals, Mihály Károlyi's [[s:hungarian-democratic-republic|Hungarian Democratic Republic]] resigned. The Social Democrats merged with the Communist Party of Béla Kun, recently released from prison, and on 21 March 1919 they proclaimed a soviet republic, governed by a Revolutionary Governing Council nominally chaired by [[e:sandor-garbai|Sándor Garbai]].
hungarian-soviet-republic.r: The regime nationalised industry, banks, large estates and housing, but kept the estates as state farms rather than giving land to peasants, losing rural support. Revolutionary tribunals and Tibor Szamuely's Lenin Boys carried out a Red Terror. A [[e:hungarian-red-army|Hungarian Red Army]] recaptured much of Slovakia in May and June, briefly creating the [[s:slovak-soviet-republic|Slovak Soviet Republic]].
hungarian-soviet-republic.e: Withdrawal from Slovakia under Allied pressure and an offensive by the Romanian army brought collapse; Kun fled to [[e:austria|Austria]] on 1 August 1919, and Romanian troops occupied [[e:budapest|Budapest]]. A [[e:white-terror-hungary|White Terror]] followed, leading to Miklós Horthy's [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1920-1946).

hajjajid-seville.t: The autonomous Arab lordship of Ibrahim ibn Hajjaj, who ruled Seville as a cultured independent prince during the late 9th-century fitna.
hajjajid-seville.o: During the breakdown of emiral authority, Arab families in [[e:seville|Seville]] fought muwallad rivals. In 899 [[e:ibrahim-ibn-hajjaj|Ibrahim ibn Hajjaj]], of the Banu Hajjaj, had his rival Kurayb ibn Khaldun killed and became master of Seville and Carmona, ruling independently of the emir [[e:abd-allah-ibn-muhammad-emir-of-cordoba|Abd Allah]].
hajjajid-seville.r: Ibrahim kept his own army, collected taxes and maintained a brilliant court in [[e:seville|Seville]], attracting poets and scholars, while sending only nominal tribute to [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]]. He allied at times with the rebel [[e:umar-ibn-hafsun|Umar ibn Hafsun]]. Seville's rich farmland along the Guadalquivir supported his power.
hajjajid-seville.e: After Ibrahim's death around 910, his sons divided his lands. [[e:abd-al-rahman-iii|Abd al-Rahman III]] recovered [[e:seville|Seville]] in 913, one of his first steps in restoring Umayyad authority across [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]].

hafsunid-bobastro.t: The mountain stronghold of the rebel Umar ibn Hafsun, whose revolt against the emirs of Córdoba lasted almost half a century.
hafsunid-bobastro.o: [[e:umar-ibn-hafsun|Umar ibn Hafsun]], a muwallad of Visigothic descent from the Málaga hills, launched a revolt around 880 and fortified Bobastro, a rocky site in the Serranía de Ronda near Ardales. Drawing support from discontented muwallads and Mozarab Christians, he soon controlled much of the mountainous south between Ronda, Málaga and Écija.
hafsunid-bobastro.r: Ibn Hafsun ruled as an independent lord, taxing his territories, building alliances with local chiefs and negotiating with the [[s:aghlabid-emirate|Aghlabids]] and [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] for recognition. Around 899 he converted to [[e:christianity|Christianity]], taking the name Samuel and building a church at Bobastro, whose rock-cut remains survive, though this lost him Muslim allies. He defeated several emiral armies but lost the battle of Poley in 891.
hafsunid-bobastro.e: After Umar's death in 917 his sons Ja'far, Sulayman and Hafs continued the struggle, but [[e:abd-al-rahman-iii|Abd al-Rahman III]] steadily reduced their fortresses. Bobastro surrendered in 928, and the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] had Umar's body exhumed and displayed in [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]].

hehe-kingdom.t: A warrior kingdom of southern Tanzania whose chief Mkwawa annihilated a German column in 1891 and resisted colonial conquest for seven years.
hehe-kingdom.o: In the mid-19th century the chief Munyigumba united the many small Hehe chiefdoms of the southern highlands by conquest and alliance, adopting military methods learned from the [[e:ngoni|Ngoni]] who had invaded the region. After his death in 1879 his son Mkwawa won a succession struggle and built the Hehe into the dominant power of the area.
hehe-kingdom.r: The Hehe state was organised for war, with regiments of spearmen and a capital at the fortified town of Kalenga. Mkwawa raided neighbours, controlled [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] to the coast and demanded tribute from traders. On 17 August 1891 his warriors destroyed a German column under Emil von Zelewski at Lugalo, one of the worst colonial defeats in [[e:east-africa|East Africa]].
hehe-kingdom.e: The Germans stormed Kalenga in 1894, and Mkwawa waged [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] war until 1898, when, cornered, he shot himself. His skull was taken to [[e:germany|Germany]] and returned to [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]] in 1954. The Hehe lands became part of [[s:german-east-africa|German East Africa]].

hoysala-empire.t: The Karnataka dynasty famous for the intricately carved temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura.
hoysala-empire.o: The Hoysalas were hill chiefs of the Malnad region of Karnataka. Legend tells how their ancestor Sala killed a tiger to protect a Jain teacher, the scene that became the dynastic emblem. In the 11th century they served as feudatories of the [[s:western-chalukya-empire|Western Chalukya Empire]], ruling from Sosevur and then [[e:dwarasamudra|Dwarasamudra]], modern Halebidu.
hoysala-empire.r: Vishnuvardhana defeated the [[s:chola-empire|Cholas]] at Talakad in 1116 and, according to tradition, turned from Jainism to Vaishnavism under the influence of the philosopher Ramanuja; he built the Chennakeshava temple at Belur. [[e:veera-ballala-ii|Veera Ballala II]] became fully independent in 1187. Hoysala temples, built of soapstone on star-shaped platforms, carry dense sculpture, as at Halebidu and Somanathapura. Kannada literature flourished, and Jain and Lingayat communities thrived alongside Vaishnavism.
hoysala-empire.e: [[e:malik-kafur|Malik Kafur]], general of [[e:alauddin-khalji|Alauddin Khalji]], sacked [[e:dwarasamudra|Dwarasamudra]] in 1311. [[e:veera-ballala-iii|Veera Ballala III]] fought on but was killed in 1343 fighting the [[s:madurai-sultanate|Madurai Sultanate]]. Former Hoysala commanders founded the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]].

hispania-baetica.t: The wealthy southern Roman province of the Guadalquivir valley, homeland of the emperors Trajan and Hadrian and of Seneca.
hispania-baetica.o: Baetica was created from the southern part of [[s:hispania-ulterior|Hispania Ulterior]] by Augustus from 27 BCE, named after the river Baetis, the Guadalquivir. It covered the former lands of the [[s:turdetani|Turdetani]] and [[s:bastetani|Bastetani]] and the old Phoenician cities, with Corduba as its capital.
hispania-baetica.r: As a peaceful, heavily urbanised region, Baetica was a public province governed by a proconsul chosen by the Senate. It exported vast amounts of [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], whose [[e:amphora|amphorae]] formed Monte Testaccio in [[e:rome|Rome]], as well as fish sauce, wine and metals. Its elite rose high: [[s:seneca-nation|Seneca]] and Lucan came from Corduba, and [[e:trajan|Trajan]] and Hadrian from Italica.
hispania-baetica.e: After the invasions of 409 the Siling [[e:vandals|Vandals]] received Baetica in 411. They were crushed by the [[e:visigoths|Visigoths]], and the Hasding Vandals passed through to [[e:africa|Africa]] in 429. Later fought over by [[s:suebi|Suebi]] and Visigoths, the region became the heartland of [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]].

hamdanid-emirate-of-aleppo.t: The Arab emirate of Sayf al-Dawla, famous for its wars against Byzantium and for a court that sheltered al-Mutanabbi and al-Farabi.
hamdanid-emirate-of-aleppo.o: The Hamdanids were a family of the Banu Taghlib who rose to power in [[e:mosul|Mosul]]. In 944-945 Ali ibn Abi'l-Hayja, known by his title [[e:sayf-al-dawla|Sayf al-Dawla]], took [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] and, after a settlement with the [[s:ikhshidid-emirate|Ikhshidids]] of [[e:egypt|Egypt]], made northern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] his own [[e:emirate|emirate]].
hamdanid-emirate-of-aleppo.r: [[e:sayf-al-dawla|Sayf al-Dawla]] spent his reign fighting [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] on the frontier, winning fame as a champion of holy war despite heavy defeats. His court gathered the poet al-Mutanabbi, his cousin the poet Abu Firas, and the philosopher al-Farabi. The dynasty was Twelver Shi'i ruling a largely [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] population and taxed heavily to fund war. In 962 [[e:nikephoros-ii-phokas|Nikephoros Phokas]] sacked [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], and in 969-970 the [[e:emirate|emirate]] became a Byzantine tributary.
hamdanid-emirate-of-aleppo.e: Under Sa'd al-Dawla and [[e:said-al-dawla|Sa'id al-Dawla]] the [[e:emirate|emirate]] was squeezed between [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]]. Real power passed to the chamberlain Lu'lu', who deposed the last Hamdanids in 1004, beginning [[s:luluid-aleppo|Lu'lu'id Aleppo]].

hellenic-republic.t: Modern Greece, the parliamentary republic founded in 1974 after the fall of the military junta, a member of the European Union since 1981.
hellenic-republic.o: The military junta that had ruled the [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]] since 1967 collapsed in July 1974 after its coup in [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] provoked a Turkish invasion. [[e:konstantinos-karamanlis|Konstantinos Karamanlis]] returned from exile to lead a civilian government, a transition known as the Metapolitefsi. In December 1974 a referendum rejected the monarchy, and a new constitution was adopted in 1975.
hellenic-republic.r: [[e:greece|Greece]] is a parliamentary republic with a president as head of state and a prime minister heading the government; politics long alternated between New Democracy and PASOK, founded by [[e:andreas-papandreou|Andreas Papandreou]]. It joined the [[e:european-economic-community|European Economic Community]] in 1981 and the euro in 2001, and hosted the 2004 [[s:athens|Athens]] Olympics. The [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox Church]] has a constitutional status.
hellenic-republic.e: The debt crisis from 2010 brought international bailouts, deep austerity and political upheaval, including the Syriza governments of 2015-2019. [[e:greece|Greece]] exited its last bailout programme in 2018 and remains a member of the [[e:european-union|European Union]] and NATO, with [[s:athens|Athens]] as its capital.

hafsid-emirate-of-bejaia.t: A breakaway Hafsid realm based at Bejaia that split the dynasty in two for a generation before its rulers reunited Ifriqiya under their own line.
hafsid-emirate-of-bejaia.o: After the death of al-Mustansir in 1277 the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsid Sultanate]] fell into succession disputes. In 1285 Abu Zakariya, a son of [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abu Ishaq Ibrahim, established himself at Bejaia and soon held Constantine and [[e:algiers|Algiers]], refusing to recognise his uncle Abu Hafs Umar in [[e:tunis|Tunis]]. The western provinces thus became a separate Hafsid state.
hafsid-emirate-of-bejaia.r: Bejaia was a prosperous port with strong ties to [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]], [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]] and Pisa, and a seat of [[e:maliki-school|Maliki]] scholarship. The [[e:emir|emirs]] governed the central [[e:maghreb|Maghreb]] through the same Almohad-style institutions as [[e:tunis|Tunis]], while facing pressure from the [[s:zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen|Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen]] on their western border and from Arab tribes in the interior.
hafsid-emirate-of-bejaia.e: Abu Zakariya's son [[e:abu-al-baqa-khalid|Abu al-Baqa Khalid]] succeeded in 1301 and, in 1309, took [[e:tunis|Tunis]], reuniting the two Hafsid realms. Bejaia and Constantine would again break away under rival princes later in the 14th century.

humbe-kingdom.t: An Nkhumbi kingdom on the Kunene river in southern Angola, a cattle-rich state that resisted Portuguese occupation until 1898.
humbe-kingdom.o: The Nkhumbi (Humbe) kingdom formed on the middle Kunene river by the 18th century, among [[e:cattle|cattle]]-keeping peoples related to the Ovambo and Nyaneka. Little is known of its early history beyond oral tradition.
humbe-kingdom.r: Kings governed through local headmen and drew their authority from [[e:cattle|cattle]] wealth and ritual. The kingdom traded cattle and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] with Portuguese and [[e:boers|Boer]] traders, while Portuguese forts established on the Kunene in the 19th century sought to tax and control it.
humbe-kingdom.e: Revolts against Portuguese demands, worsened by the rinderpest epidemic of 1897 that destroyed herds, were suppressed in 1898, when Portugal took control of the kingdom and absorbed it into [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]].

hahhum.t: Hahhum, a wealthy city at a crossing of the upper Euphrates, an Assyrian trade station later sacked by the Hittite king Hattusili I.
hahhum.o: Hahhum lay on the upper [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]], probably near Samsat in south-eastern [[e:turkey|Turkey]], where the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] from [[e:assur|Assur]] crossed the river into [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. It appears in the Old Assyrian letters of the 19th century BCE as a stopping place with its own ruler and merchant community.
hahhum.r: Little is known of how it was governed. Its wealth came from controlling the river crossing and charging caravans, and it seems to have been allied with the Hurrian and Syrian powers to its south.
hahhum.e: In the 17th century BCE [[e:hattusili-i|Hattusili I]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] crossed the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]], burned Hahhum and carried its gods to [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]], boasting that he had surpassed [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon of Akkad]]. The city does not reappear as a kingdom.

hadeland.t: Small inland kingdom on Lake Randsfjorden, linked in saga tradition to Halfdan the Black and ended when Olaf Haraldsson removed the Uppland kings.
hadeland.o: Hadeland, a farming district around the southern end of Lake Randsfjorden, was one of the petty kingdoms of the Upplands of eastern [[e:norway|Norway]]. [[e:snorri-sturluson|Snorri Sturluson's]] sagas say it was won by [[e:halfdan-the-black|Halfdan the Black]], father of [[e:harald-fairhair|Harald Fairhair]], in the 9th century.
hadeland.r: Little is known of its government. The sagas tell that [[e:halfdan-the-black|Halfdan the Black]] drowned when his sleigh broke through the ice on Randsfjorden, and that the districts quarrelled over his body, which was divided and buried in several places. Local kings continued to hold the district under the Norwegian high kings.
hadeland.e: Around 1018 [[e:olaf-ii-of-norway|Olaf Haraldsson]] defeated a coalition of the Uppland kings, including the king of Hadeland, and took their lands into his kingdom. Hadeland became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]], and the twin medieval churches at Granavollen are among its later landmarks.

hazaraspid-dynasty.t: A Lur dynasty that ruled Greater Luristan, the mountainous Bakhtiari country of south-western Iran, for nearly three centuries.
hazaraspid-dynasty.o: The dynasty's founder, [[e:abu-tahir-ibn-muhammad|Abu Tahir ibn Muhammad]], was a Kurdish or Lur commander in the service of the [[s:salghurid-dynasty|Salghurid dynasty]] of [[e:fars|Fars]]. Around 1148 he was sent to subdue the region of Lur-i Buzurg (Greater Luristan) and made himself its ruler. His son Hazarasp gave the dynasty its name.
hazaraspid-dynasty.r: The Hazaraspids ruled from Idhaj (modern Izeh) over a land of transhumant tribes, valleys and mountain pastures. They styled themselves atabegs and built mosques, [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] and [[e:sufism|Sufi]] lodges. Yusuf Shah I and Afrasiyab I were among the notable rulers, the latter known for his brutality. The dynasty survived by submitting to the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]], the [[s:muzaffarid-dynasty|Muzaffarid dynasty]] and then [[e:timur|Timur]].
hazaraspid-dynasty.e: In 1424 the Timurid prince Ibrahim [[e:sultan|Sultan]], governor of [[e:fars|Fars]], deposed the last Hazaraspid ruler, ending the dynasty. Its lands later formed the [[s:bakhtiari-confederation|Bakhtiari]] country, home of the [[e:bakhtiari|Bakhtiari]] confederation.

helvii.t: Gallic people of the Vivarais who stayed loyal to Rome in 52 BCE and from whose land Caesar crossed the snowbound Cévennes.
helvii.o: The Helvii lived on the right bank of the Rhône in the modern Ardèche, at the edge of the [[e:massif-central|Massif Central]]. Their land became part of the Roman Province after 121 BCE.
helvii.r: Caesar names Gaius Valerius Caburus, who had received Roman citizenship from the governor Gaius Valerius Flaccus, an early example of a Gallic noble family adopting Roman ways. His son [[e:gaius-valerius-donnotaurus|Gaius Valerius Donnotaurus]] was the leading man of the people in 52 BCE.
helvii.e: In 52 BCE the Helvii were attacked by the [[s:gabali|Gabali]] and [[s:arverni|Arverni]] for their loyalty, and Donnotaurus was killed in the fighting. Caesar marched through their territory and crossed the Cévennes in deep snow to strike the Arverni. Their Roman town was Alba Helviorum (Alba-la-Romaine), and the region later became the Vivarais.

harar-emirate.t: A walled Muslim city-state in eastern Ethiopia, a centre of Islamic learning and trade, which kept its independence until Menelik II took it in 1887.
harar-emirate.o: After the Adal leadership moved to the [[s:imamate-of-aussa|Imamate of Aussa]], [[e:harar|Harar]] was left to local governors. In 1647 [[e:emir|Emir]] Ali ibn Daud founded an independent dynasty, ruling the city and its farmlands amid the Oromo-settled countryside. The city walls, built in the 16th century by Emir [[e:nur-ibn-mujahid|Nur ibn Mujahid]], enclosed the old town of [[e:jugol|Jugol]].
harar-emirate.r: [[e:harar|Harar]] was a city of mosques, shrines and scholars, its own [[e:harari|Harari]] language written in Arabic script. The [[e:emir|emirs]] minted coins and taxed the caravans carrying [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], khat, slaves and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] to [[e:zeila|Zeila]] and Berbera. They made alliances with surrounding [[e:oromo|Oromo]] groups. Richard Burton, the first European known to enter, visited in 1855.
harar-emirate.e: [[e:egypt|Egypt]] occupied [[e:harar|Harar]] from 1875 to 1885, after which [[e:emir|Emir]] Abdullahi ibn Ali briefly restored independence. [[e:menelik-ii|Menelik II]] defeated him at the Battle of Chelenqo in 1887 and annexed Harar to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]]. The old walled town is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

hospitaller-malta.t: The crusading Order of Saint John's island state, which defeated the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565 and built Valletta.
hospitaller-malta.o: Expelled from [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] by the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] in 1522, the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]] received Malta, Gozo and [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] from [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Charles V]] in 1530, in return for a symbolic annual falcon. Grand Master [[e:philippe-villiers-de-lisle-adam|Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam]] settled the Order at Birgu.
hospitaller-malta.r: The Order, a military-religious brotherhood of European nobles divided into national langues, was ruled by an elected Grand Master. In 1565 [[e:jean-parisot-de-valette|Jean de Valette]] defended Malta against the Ottoman Great Siege, and the new capital Valletta was built from 1566. The knights waged corsair war on Muslim shipping, ran a celebrated hospital, the Sacra Infermeria, and built fortifications, churches and palaces.
hospitaller-malta.e: In 1798 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] fleet, on its way to [[e:egypt|Egypt]], demanded entry; Grand Master Ferdinand von Hompesch surrendered without a fight. The French were expelled in 1800, and Malta became a British possession. The Order survives as a sovereign body in [[e:rome|Rome]].

hadiya-sultanate.t: A Muslim state of the southern Ethiopian highlands that alternated between tribute to the Christian emperors and alliance with Adal.
hadiya-sultanate.o: Hadiya is first mentioned in Arabic and Ethiopian sources in the 13th century as a Muslim state southwest of [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]], on routes bringing slaves and goods north to [[e:zeila|Zeila]]. Its people spoke Hadiyya, a Highland East Cushitic language. In 1332 its ruler Amano was defeated by the emperor [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] and made tributary to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]].
hadiya-sultanate.r: Hadiya was ruled by a garad or sultan and supplied troops to the Christian emperors in return for autonomy. Its trade in slaves and horses made it valuable to both sides. Relations were tense: Garad Mahiko rebelled against [[e:zara-yaqob|Zara Yaqob]] in the 15th century, while a Hadiya princess, Eleni, married the emperor and became a powerful empress dowager.
hadiya-sultanate.e: Hadiya joined the [[e:jihad|jihad]] of [[e:ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi|Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi]] of Adal in the 1530s, and was then broken up by the [[e:oromo-migrations|Oromo migrations]] of the 16th century. The Hadiya people still live in southern [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]], where a zone bears their name.

hasanlu.t: A fortified Iron Age town south of Lake Urmia, frozen in time by its violent destruction around 800 BCE, which preserved its famous gold bowl.
hasanlu.o: Hasanlu Tepe had been occupied since the Neolithic, but its best-known phase, Hasanlu IV, dates from about 1100 to 800 BCE, when a fortified citadel with columned halls dominated the Solduz valley. Some scholars identify it with Gilzanu or a centre of the people later known as [[s:mannaea|Mannaea]].
hasanlu.r: The citadel held temples or palace halls with wooden pillars, storerooms of horse gear, weapons and [[e:ivory-trade|ivories]], and evidence of contacts with [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and the [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]]. The Hasanlu gold bowl, decorated with mythological scenes, is its most famous find. Its rulers, language and political structure are unknown, since no local texts survive; the community seems to have been an elite of horse-riding warriors controlling the valley.
hasanlu.e: Around 800 BCE the citadel was stormed and burnt, probably by the [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Kingdom of Urartu]] expanding south. Penn Museum excavations under Robert Dyson (1956 to 1977) found hundreds of bodies, including the pair known as the 'Hasanlu Lovers'.

hassum.t: Hassum, a wealthy kingdom west of the upper Euphrates, ally of Aleppo, whose gods were carried off to Hattusa by the Hittite king Hattusili I.
hassum.o: Hashshum lay in the borderlands of northern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and south-eastern [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], west of the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]]. It is mentioned in the Old Assyrian trade letters and the [[s:mari|Mari]] archives as a kingdom on the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]], closely tied to [[s:yamhad|Yamhad]].
hassum.r: Little is known of its internal government. The texts show it as a prosperous city with temples of the storm god and his consort Hebat, reflecting the Hurrian and Syrian culture of the region.
hassum.e: In the 17th century BCE [[e:hattusili-i|Hattusili I]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] defeated the armies of Hassum and [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], sacked the city and carried its divine statues, wagons and treasures to the temple of the sun goddess of Arinna.

hilakku.t: Hilakku, a land of mountain chiefs in Rough Cilicia that resisted Assyrian armies and gave its name to Cilicia.
hilakku.o: Hilakku was the Assyrian name for the rugged [[e:taurus-mountains|Taurus]] country of western [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]], behind the coast of modern Mersin. It appears in Assyrian sources from the 9th century BCE as a land of local rulers, west of the plain of Que.
hilakku.r: Little is known of its government. Its people raided the lowlands and resisted Assyrian control from mountain strongholds. In 696 BCE [[e:sennacherib|Sennacherib]] put down a revolt led by Kirua, ruler of Illubru, and later Sanda-sharme of Hilakku sent his daughter to the harem of [[e:ashurbanipal|Ashurbanipal]].
hilakku.e: Hilakku remained outside firm Assyrian rule, and after [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria's]] fall its lands formed part of the [[s:kingdom-of-cilicia|Kingdom of Cilicia]]. Its name survived in Greek as Kilikia.

hattum.t: Hattum, the Hattian city-state on the site of later Hattusa, cursed and destroyed by Anitta before it rose again as the Hittite capital.
hattum.o: Hattus was a native Hattian town on a rocky ridge near modern Boğazkale in central [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. By the early 2nd millennium BCE it was the seat of a local king and hosted a small trading quarter of merchants from [[e:assur|Assur]], part of the network centred on [[s:kanesh|Kanesh]].
hattum.r: Little is known of its government beyond Old Assyrian letters and the later Hittite tradition. Its people spoke Hattic, a language unrelated to Hittite or Semitic tongues, and their gods, such as the sun goddess of Arinna, were later absorbed into Hittite religion.
hattum.e: Around 1730 BCE [[e:anitta|Anitta of Kussara]] took the city after its king Piyusti was defeated, razed it and sowed it with weeds, cursing any king who resettled it. A century later [[e:hattusili-i|Hattusili I]] did exactly that, making [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]] the capital of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]].

hamdanid-emirate-of-mosul.t: The Arab emirate of the Taghlib family of Hamdan in northern Iraq, whose ruler Nasir al-Dawla briefly controlled the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad.
hamdanid-emirate-of-mosul.o: The Hamdanids, from the Arab tribe of Taghlib in the Jazira, rose as Abbasid commanders. In 905 Abu'l-Hayja Abdallah ibn Hamdan was appointed governor of [[e:mosul|Mosul]]. His son al-Hasan, given the title [[e:nasir-al-dawla|Nasir al-Dawla]] in 942, turned the governorship into a hereditary [[e:emirate|emirate]] over Mosul and the Diyar Rabi'a.
hamdanid-emirate-of-mosul.r: [[e:nasir-al-dawla|Nasir al-Dawla]] was briefly amir al-umara, effective master of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] and the [[e:caliphate|caliph]], in 942 to 943, and later fought the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyid dynasty]] for control of [[e:iraq|Iraq]]. He was known for heavy taxation of the Jazira's farmland. His brother [[e:sayf-al-dawla|Sayf al-Dawla]] founded the [[s:hamdanid-emirate-of-aleppo|Hamdanid Emirate of Aleppo]], famed for its court poets such as al-Mutanabbi. The family favoured [[e:shia-islam|Shia Islam]] while ruling a mixed [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] and Christian population.
hamdanid-emirate-of-mosul.e: [[e:nasir-al-dawla|Nasir al-Dawla]] was deposed by his son [[e:abu-taghlib|Abu Taghlib]] in 967. In 978 [[e:adud-al-dawla|Adud al-Dawla]] of the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyids]] expelled the Hamdanids from [[e:mosul|Mosul]]; a brief return ended around 990, when the [[s:uqaylid-dynasty|Uqaylid dynasty]] took over.

halin.t: A walled Pyu city in the Mu valley of upper Myanmar, a centre of salt and rice production until it was sacked by Nanzhao in 832.
halin.o: Halin, also called Halingyi, near Shwebo in the [[s:sagaing-kingdom|Sagaing]] region, developed as a Pyu city from around the 1st century CE, though finds at the site go back to the [[e:bronze|Bronze]] and [[e:iron-age|Iron Ages]]. It was enclosed by a brick wall around 10 km long.
halin.r: Halin drew wealth from irrigated [[e:rice|rice]] and local salt production, and Pyu inscriptions found there record its rulers and their Buddhist donations. Excavations have uncovered a palace area, stupas, urn burials and gold and [[e:silver|silver]] objects. It was one of the larger Pyu cities and may have been the leading centre after [[s:sri-ksetra-kingdom|Sri Ksetra]]'s decline.
halin.e: Chinese records say that troops of [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] attacked the Pyu in 832 and carried off thousands of captives, and Halin is usually identified as the city they sacked. The site was later occupied on a smaller scale. It is part of the Pyu ancient cities [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].

hamazi.t: A shadowy early kingdom in the hills east of the Tigris, listed among the holders of kingship in the Sumerian King List and in contact with distant Ebla.
hamazi.o: Hamazi is known only from a handful of texts, and even its location is uncertain; most scholars place it in the [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]] foothills between the Diyala and the [[e:little-zab|Lesser Zab]], perhaps near modern Sulaymaniyah. It appears in the [[e:early-dynastic-period|Early Dynastic period]], around the 25th century BCE.
hamazi.r: The [[e:sumerian-king-list|Sumerian King List]] records a single king, Hadanish, as holding kingship for Hamazi before it passed to [[s:uruk|Uruk]]. A letter from the archives of [[s:ebla|Ebla]] in [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], sent to a ruler named Zizi of Hamazi, shows that the kingdom was part of a long-distance diplomatic network and exchanged gifts with Syrian courts. Nothing is known of its society, language or religion beyond these mentions.
hamazi.e: Hamazi disappears from the sources by the Akkadian period, presumably absorbed by stronger neighbours or by the [[e:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire's]] campaigns in the [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]]. A late [[e:third-dynasty-of-ur|Ur III]] text mentions people of Hamazi, but no later state of the name is known.

hayato.t: The people of southern Kyushu who resisted incorporation into the early Japanese state until their great rebellion was crushed in 720.
hayato.o: The Hayato lived in the [[e:satsuma-domain|Satsuma]] and Osumi regions of southern Kyushu and are often linked to the Kumaso of earlier legend. They appear in court records from the late 7th century as a frontier people paying tribute to the [[s:yamato|Yamato court]].
hayato.r: Their society was organised in local groups under chiefs, and their customs, language and dress were considered foreign by the court. Groups of Hayato were brought to the capital to serve as guards and perform ritual dances and chants at court ceremonies. The imposition of ritsuryo provinces and land registers on their territory provoked resistance.
hayato.e: A major rebellion broke out in 720 and was suppressed after more than a year by an army under Otomo no Tabito. Southern Kyushu was then integrated into the provincial system; Hayato tribute missions ended in 801, though Hayato still served at court ceremonies in the 9th century.

huan-chu.t: The brief usurping dynasty of Huan Xuan, who seized the Eastern Jin throne at Jiankang in 403 and was overthrown by Liu Yu within months.
huan-chu.o: [[e:huan-xuan|Huan Xuan]] was the son of the great general [[e:huan-wen|Huan Wen]] and controlled Jing province on the middle [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]]. In 402 he marched on Jiankang, overthrowing the regent Sima Daozi's family, and in 403 he forced [[e:emperor-an-of-jin|Emperor An]] of the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]] to abdicate and proclaimed himself emperor of Chu.
huan-chu.r: [[e:huan-xuan|Huan Xuan]] was a cultivated aristocrat and collector of [[e:calligraphy|calligraphy]], but his rule was erratic, marked by grandiose building and constant changes of policy. He lacked the loyalty of the Beifu army, the main northern military force.
huan-chu.e: In 404 [[e:emperor-wu-of-liu-song|Liu Yu]] and other Beifu officers rose at Jingkou and took Jiankang. [[e:huan-xuan|Huan Xuan]] fled west with the captive [[e:emperor-an-of-jin|Emperor An]] and was killed. The [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]] was restored under Liu Yu's control, the first step towards his founding of the [[s:liu-song|Liu Song]].

helvetii.t: Celtic confederation of the Swiss plateau whose attempted mass migration in 58 BCE triggered Caesar's conquest of Gaul.
helvetii.o: [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] says the Helvetii once lived between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the Main before moving to the Swiss plateau between the Jura and the [[e:alps|Alps]]. They were divided into four cantons, and one of them, the Tigurini under Divico, joined the Cimbri and defeated a Roman army near Agen in 107 BCE.
helvetii.r: They lived in fortified oppida and villages and were governed by a nobility. The site of [[e:la-tene-culture|La Tène]] on Lake Neuchâtel, with its weapons and offerings, has given its name to the late [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] culture of Celtic [[e:europe|Europe]].
helvetii.e: Following a plan of the noble Orgetorix, who died before it began, they burned their towns and set off west in 58 BCE, but Caesar defeated them near Bibracte and sent the survivors home. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Aventicum (Avenches) became their capital, and modern [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] still calls itself Confoederatio Helvetica.

hospitaller-tripoli.t: Tripoli under the Knights of St John, a reluctant outpost they held for two decades before losing it to the Ottoman fleet in 1551.
hospitaller-tripoli.o: In 1530 [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] granted Malta and [[s:spanish-tripoli|Spanish Tripoli]] to the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]], homeless since losing [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] in 1522. The Order accepted [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] unwillingly, as it was exposed and expensive, but took over the garrison under its own governors.
hospitaller-tripoli.r: The knights ruled from the old castle, strengthening its walls and using the port as a base for [[e:galley|galleys]] against Muslim shipping. Their small force depended on supplies from [[s:hospitaller-malta|Hospitaller Malta]] and [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. Relations with the surrounding Arab population and with the corsair [[e:turgut-reis|Turgut Reis]] at Tajura were hostile.
hospitaller-tripoli.e: In August 1551 an Ottoman fleet under [[e:sinan-pasha-ottoman-admiral|Sinan Pasha]] and [[e:turgut-reis|Turgut Reis]] besieged [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]]. The governor [[e:gaspard-de-vallier|Gaspard de Vallier]] surrendered after a brief bombardment, and the city became [[s:ottoman-tripolitania|Ottoman Tripolitania]].

hunnic-empire.t: The nomadic empire whose arrival in Europe set the Goths in motion and which, under Attila, held both halves of the Roman Empire to ransom.
hunnic-empire.o: The [[e:huns|Huns]] appeared north of the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] around 370, defeating the [[s:alans|Alans]] and then the [[s:greuthungi|Greuthungi]] Goths of Ermanaric, which drove the [[s:tervingi|Tervingi]] across the [[e:danube|Danube]] into Roman territory. Their origins further east are uncertain, though many scholars connect them with the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]]. By the 420s they had moved their centre to the Hungarian plain.
hunnic-empire.r: Hun power rested on [[e:mounted-archer|mounted archers]] and on a confederation of subject peoples, including Goths, Gepids, [[s:alans|Alans]] and the [[s:akatziri|Akatziri]]. Kings such as Rua, and then the brothers Bleda and Attila, extracted huge annual payments in gold from [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] through treaties such as that of Margus in 435. Priscus, who visited Attila's court in 449, describes wooden palaces, Gothic and [[e:latin|Latin]] speakers, and an elite enriched by tribute and plunder.
hunnic-empire.e: After Attila's defeat at the [[e:battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains|Catalaunian Plains]] in 451, his raid on [[e:italy|Italy]] in 452 and his death in 453, the subject peoples revolted under the Gepid king Ardaric and won at the Nedao in 454. Attila's son Dengizich was killed in 469, and the remaining [[e:huns|Huns]] merged into later steppe peoples.

herodian-kingdom-of-judea.t: The kingdom of Herod the Great, a Roman client state that rebuilt Jerusalem's Temple and left fortresses like Masada.
herodian-kingdom-of-judea.o: Herod, an Idumaean noble whose father had served Hasmonean rulers, was named king of Judea by the [[s:commune-of-rome|Roman Senate]] in 40 BCE. With Roman help he captured [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]] from [[e:antigonus-i-monophthalmus|Antigonus]], last of the [[s:hasmonean-kingdom|Hasmonean Kingdom]], in 37 BCE.
herodian-kingdom-of-judea.r: Herod ruled as a loyal client of [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony]] and then Augustus. He rebuilt the Temple on a vast platform, founded the harbour city of [[s:lordship-of-caesarea|Caesarea]] [[s:laanemaa|Maritima]] and built palaces at Masada and Herodium. His rule was harsh and suspicious; he executed his wife Mariamne and several of his sons.
herodian-kingdom-of-judea.e: After Herod's death in 4 BCE, Augustus divided the kingdom among his sons Archelaus, [[e:herod-antipas|Herod Antipas]] and Philip. Judea itself became a Roman province in 6 CE.

histri.t: Iron Age people of the Istrian peninsula, centred on Nesactium, whose resistance to Rome ended with the fall of their stronghold in 177 BCE.
histri.o: The Histri, who gave their name to [[s:histria|Istria]], emerged from the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] hillfort culture of the peninsula in the early first millennium BCE. Rich graves at Nesactium near Pula show a wealthy elite with links to [[e:italy|Italy]], the [[s:ancient-veneti|Veneti]] and the Adriatic by the 6th century BCE.
histri.r: A king ruled from Nesactium over hillforts (castellieri) scattered across the peninsula. The Histri farmed, kept herds and were notorious to [[e:rome|Rome]] as [[e:piracy|pirates]] preying on Adriatic shipping. Stone sculpture at Nesactium, including figures of riders and mothers, shows a distinctive local art influenced by Italian and Greek styles.
histri.e: Roman campaigns began in 221 BCE after attacks on grain ships. After the founding of Aquileia in 181 BCE war resumed, and in 177 BCE the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher stormed Nesactium; King Epulo killed himself. [[s:histria|Istria]] was later joined to [[e:italy|Italy]] under Augustus.

ho-dynasty.t: A seven-year Vietnamese dynasty of radical reformer Ho Quy Ly, who issued paper money and built a stone citadel before the Ming conquest.
ho-dynasty.o: [[e:ho-quy-ly|Ho Quy Ly]], a powerful minister related by marriage to the [[s:tran-dynasty|Tran dynasty]], dominated the court in the 1390s, moved the capital to a new stone citadel at Tay Do in [[e:thanh-hoa|Thanh Hoa]] and in 1400 deposed the last Tran emperor. He renamed the state Dai Ngu and soon passed the throne to his son [[e:ho-han-thuong|Ho Han Thuong]].
ho-dynasty.r: [[e:ho-quy-ly|Ho Quy Ly]] pursued sweeping reforms: he limited private landholdings and the number of slaves, introduced [[e:paper-money|paper money]], reformed the examinations to favour practical learning, and promoted chu nom. The Citadel of the Ho Dynasty, built of huge cut stone blocks, is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]]. His usurpation alienated many Tran loyalists.
ho-dynasty.e: Using the overthrow of the Tran as a pretext, the [[e:yongle-emperor|Yongle Emperor]] sent a Ming army in 1406. Dai Ngu collapsed within a year; [[e:ho-quy-ly|Ho Quy Ly]] and his son were captured in 1407 and taken to [[e:china|China]], and [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] became Jiaozhi Province.

hipponion.t: Colony of Locri on the Tyrrhenian coast of Calabria, known for an Orphic gold tablet, which became the Roman colony of Vibo Valentia in 192 BCE.
hipponion.o: [[s:locri-epizephyrii|Locri Epizephyrii]] founded Hipponion in the 7th century BCE on a hill above the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia, giving the Locrians a port on the [[e:tyrrhenian-sea|Tyrrhenian Sea]] and a share in the trade crossing the Calabrian isthmus.
hipponion.r: Hipponion depended on [[s:locri-epizephyrii|Locri]] for much of its history and shared its alliances. It had temples, a city wall and a port. A gold leaf found in a woman's grave of about 400 BCE gives Orphic instructions for the soul in the underworld and is a key text for Greek mystery religion.
hipponion.e: Dionysius I destroyed Hipponion in 389 BCE and moved its people to [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]], but [[e:carthage|Carthage]] restored them in 379 BCE. The [[s:bruttii|Bruttii]] captured it around 356 BCE, and Agathocles briefly held it. [[e:rome|Rome]] founded the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of [[e:vibo-valentia|Vibo Valentia]] there in 192 BCE, today's Vibo Valentia.

ha-tien-principality.t: A semi-independent trading port on the Gulf of Thailand founded by the Chinese exile Mac Cuu, which bridged Cambodia, Vietnam and Siam.
ha-tien-principality.o: [[e:mac-cuu|Mac Cuu]], a Ming loyalist from Guangdong, settled at [[e:ha-tien|Ha Tien]], then a Cambodian coastal town called Peam, in the late 17th century and developed it into a trading port with Cambodian approval. Around 1707 to 1708 he submitted to the [[s:nguyen-lords|Nguyen lords]], who confirmed him as governor.
ha-tien-principality.r: [[e:ha-tien|Ha Tien]] was run by the Mac family as a hereditary principality with its own army and fleet, trading [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:timber|timber]] and goods across the Gulf with Siam, [[e:batavia|Batavia]] and [[e:china|China]]. Under Mac Thien Tu it became a cultural centre where Chinese and Vietnamese poets gathered, and its rulers intervened in Cambodian successions.
ha-tien-principality.e: Taksin of the [[s:thonburi-kingdom|Thonburi Kingdom]] sacked [[e:ha-tien|Ha Tien]] in 1771, and the [[e:tay-son-dynasty|Tay Son]] wars further damaged it. Members of the Mac family continued as governors under the [[s:nguyen-dynasty|Nguyen dynasty]] into the early 19th century, and the territory was fully incorporated into [[e:vietnam|Vietnam's]] provincial system by 1832.

hlubi-chiefdom.t: A northern Nguni chiefdom scattered in the wars of the early 19th century, remembered for Langalibalele's 1873 confrontation with colonial Natal.
hlubi-chiefdom.o: The Hlubi were an [[e:nguni|Nguni]] chiefdom settled near the upper Mzinyathi (Buffalo) river in what is now northern KwaZulu-Natal. By the late 18th century, under Bhungane, they were among the larger chiefdoms of the region.
hlubi-chiefdom.r: Hlubi chiefs ruled over [[e:cattle|cattle]]-herding homesteads, and their royal house was famed for rainmaking. Around 1818 the Hlubi were attacked by the [[s:swazi-kingdom|Ngwane]] and later the [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]]; one section under Mpangazitha fled onto the highveld and fought in the wars of the 1820s. Others later settled in [[s:natal-colony|Natal]] under Langalibalele, a renowned rainmaker.
hlubi-chiefdom.e: In 1873 Langalibalele refused to register guns his men had earned at the diamond fields; the [[s:natal-colony|Natal]] government declared him in rebellion, broke up the Hlubi location and sent him to Robben Island. The Hlubi chieftaincy was later restored.

himeji-domain.t: The domain centred on Himeji castle, the great white keep that Ikeda Terumasa built and that survives as Japan's finest original castle.
himeji-domain.o: After [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]], [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave Harima to his son-in-law [[e:ikeda-terumasa|Ikeda Terumasa]] with 520,000 koku in 1600. Between 1601 and 1609 Terumasa rebuilt Himeji castle on the site of an earlier fortress, creating the present complex of white-plastered towers.
himeji-domain.r: Himeji guarded the western approaches to [[e:kyoto|Kyoto]], so the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] placed trusted families there and moved them often. [[e:honda-tadamasa|Honda Tadamasa]], whose wife was Senhime, granddaughter of [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Ieyasu]], held it from 1617. The [[s:sakai|Sakai]] family ruled from 1749 to the end, and the reformer Kawai Sundo restored finances through a domain monopoly on [[e:cotton|cotton]].
himeji-domain.e: Because its lord [[e:sakai-tadashige|Sakai Tadashige]] was the [[e:shogun|shogun]]'s great elder, Himeji was treated as an enemy in 1868 and surrendered when besieged by imperial forces. It became part of Hyogo Prefecture in 1871, and the castle became a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]] in 1993.

halicarnassus.t: Greek and Carian port city, birthplace of Herodotus and home of Queen Artemisia, which became the capital of Mausolus and the site of his Mausoleum.
halicarnassus.o: Halicarnassus was founded by Dorian settlers from [[s:troezen|Troezen]] on a bay of the Carian coast, beside native Carian communities, and the two populations mixed. It belonged to the [[e:dorian-hexapolis|Dorian Hexapolis]] but, according to [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]], was expelled after one of its citizens carried off a prize tripod.
halicarnassus.r: Under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] it was ruled by a Carian-Greek dynasty: Lygdamis I and his daughter Artemisia I, who commanded ships for [[e:xerxes-i|Xerxes]] at Salamis in 480 BCE. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]], born there, opposed [[e:lygdamis-ii|Lygdamis II]] and went into exile. After the tyranny ended, Halicarnassus joined the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]].
halicarnassus.e: [[e:mausolus|Mausolus of Hecatomnid Caria]] made Halicarnassus his capital in the 370s BCE, absorbing it into his dynastic state; his tomb, the Mausoleum, was a Wonder of the World. Alexander besieged the city in 334 BCE. It is modern Bodrum.

hamdanid-sultanate-of-yemen.t: A dynasty of the Hamdan tribe that ruled Sanaa in the 12th century after the breakup of the Sulayhid state.
hamdanid-sultanate-of-yemen.o: After the [[s:sulayhid-dynasty|Sulayhid dynasty]] lost control of the highlands, leaders of the Hamdan tribe took Sanaa. In 1099 Hatim ibn al-Ghashim established the dynasty that ruled the city, with brief interruptions, for most of the 12th century.
hamdanid-sultanate-of-yemen.r: Three branches of the family succeeded one another in Sanaa. They were Isma'ilis loyal to the Hafizi [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] and spent much effort fighting Zaydi [[e:imam|imams]] to the north and local rivals. Their state was essentially a tribal confederation around Sanaa and its forts. Little is known of its administration beyond chronicles of war.
hamdanid-sultanate-of-yemen.e: In 1174 the Ayyubid prince Turan-Shah invaded [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]]. [[e:ali-ibn-hatim|Ali ibn Hatim]] fled to the mountains, and by the 1180s Sanaa was under [[s:ayyubid-yemen|Ayyubid Yemen]]. The dynasty's fall marked the end of Isma'ili political rule in [[e:yemen|Yemen]].

han-zhao.t: The first of the Sixteen Kingdoms, founded by the Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan, whose armies sacked Luoyang in 311 and destroyed the Western Jin.
han-zhao.o: [[e:liu-yuan|Liu Yuan]], a descendant of the [[s:southern-xiongnu|Southern Xiongnu]] shanyus educated in the Chinese classics, rebelled during the [[e:war-of-the-eight-princes|War of the Eight Princes]]. In 304 he proclaimed himself King of Han, claiming the [[e:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty's]] legacy through ancestral marriages between Han princesses and shanyus. He became emperor in 308 and in 309 moved his capital to Pingyang in [[e:shanxi|Shanxi]].
han-zhao.r: The state ruled Chinese subjects through a Chinese-style bureaucracy and the tribes through a separate [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]] hierarchy. Liu Cong's generals, including [[e:shi-le|Shi Le]] and [[e:liu-yao|Liu Yao]], captured [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] in 311 and [[e:changan|Chang'an]] in 316, taking two Jin emperors prisoner. After a coup in 318, Liu Yao moved the capital to Chang'an and renamed the state Zhao.
han-zhao.e: [[e:shi-le|Shi Le]], who had broken away to found [[s:later-zhao|Later Zhao]], captured [[e:liu-yao|Liu Yao]] at [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] in 328. [[e:changan|Chang'an]] fell in 329 and the dynasty was wiped out. Han Zhao began three centuries in which northern [[e:china|China]] was ruled by dynasties of steppe origin.

hariphunchai.t: A Mon Buddhist kingdom in northern Thailand, founded according to legend by Queen Chamadevi, which survived until Mangrai of Lan Na took it in 1292.
hariphunchai.o: Northern Thai chronicles say that the hermit founders of Hariphunchai at Lamphun invited Chamadevi, a princess of Lavo, to rule the new city, traditionally in the 7th century. She brought Mon Buddhist monks and craftsmen from the [[s:dvaravati|Dvaravati]] world, and one of her twin sons founded [[s:principality-of-lampang|Lampang]] as a second centre.
hariphunchai.r: Hariphunchai was a Mon-speaking Buddhist kingdom that kept [[s:dvaravati|Dvaravati]] traditions alive long after they faded in the south. [[e:old-mon|Old Mon]] inscriptions from the 12th and 13th centuries record its kings' merit-making, and King Adityaraja is credited with building the Wat Phra That Hariphunchai stupa. It fought repeated wars with Lavo and the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]].
hariphunchai.e: In 1292 [[e:mangrai|Mangrai]] of [[s:ngoenyang|Ngoenyang]] captured Lamphun through a ruse and incorporated it into his new kingdom of [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]]. Hariphunchai's Buddhist learning and Mon script shaped the culture of Lan Na, and Lamphun's great stupa remains a major pilgrimage site.

hawwara-emirate.t: The domain of the Hawwara sheikhs, Arabised Berber lords who ruled most of Upper Egypt under Ottoman sovereignty until 1769.
hawwara-emirate.o: The Hawwara, a tribe of [[e:berbers|Berber]] origin, were resettled in [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]] by the [[s:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Sultanate]] in the late 14th century. Under [[s:ottoman-egypt|Ottoman Egypt]] their sheikhs became the dominant power in the south, with their seat at Farshut near Qena, and from the later 16th century they acted as tax farmers and governors of Upper [[e:egypt|Egypt]].
hawwara-emirate.r: The Hawwara sheikhs controlled vast estates producing grain and [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] cane, collecting taxes for [[e:cairo|Cairo]] and keeping order among the tribes. Their court at Farshut was known for hospitality and patronage. At its height under Shaykh Hammam ibn Yusuf, in the mid-18th century, their authority stretched over much of the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley from [[e:asyut|Asyut]] to Aswan.
hawwara-emirate.e: Hammam sheltered [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] rivals of [[e:ali-bey-al-kabir|Ali Bey al-Kabir]]. In 1769 Ali Bey's forces under Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab defeated the Hawwara, and Hammam died in flight, ending their autonomous power in [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]].

hindol-state.t: One of the small tributary Garhjat states of Orissa, ruled by a Raja from its hill-ringed seat in the Mahanadi uplands.
hindol-state.o: Hindol lay in the forested hills north of the Mahanadi, in today's [[s:dhenkanal-state|Dhenkanal]] district. Its ruling family's traditions date the state to the mid-16th century, when chiefs from neighbouring houses carved out holdings among the tribal hill country of central Orissa.
hindol-state.r: The Raja ruled a population of Oriya peasants and tribal communities, drawing revenue from [[e:rice|rice]] cultivation and forest produce. After the British conquest of Orissa in 1803 Hindol became one of the [[e:orissa-tributary-states|Orissa Tributary Mahals]], later grouped in the [[e:eastern-states-agency|Eastern States Agency]].
hindol-state.e: Following widespread popular agitation (the [[e:praja-mandal|Praja Mandal]] movement) in the Orissa states, its ruler signed the merger agreement and Hindol joined the province of Orissa on 1 January 1948.

hausa-kingdoms.t: The family of walled Hausa city-kingdoms between the Niger and Lake Chad, which for eight centuries dominated the trade and crafts of the central Sudan.
hausa-kingdoms.o: Hausa-speaking communities on the savanna of what is now northern [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]] and southern [[e:niger-river|Niger]] formed walled towns, or birane, around the end of the first millennium. Tradition groups them as the [[e:hausa|Hausa]] Bakwai, the seven 'legitimate' states descended from Bayajidda ([[s:kingdom-of-daura|Daura]], [[e:kano|Kano]], [[s:katsina-kingdom|Katsina]], [[s:kingdom-of-zazzau|Zazzau]], [[s:kingdom-of-gobir|Gobir]], Rano and [[s:kingdom-of-biram|Biram]]), and the [[e:banza-bakwai|Banza Bakwai]], seven others including [[s:kingdom-of-zamfara|Zamfara]], [[s:kingdom-of-kebbi|Kebbi]], [[s:kingdom-of-yauri|Yauri]] and [[e:nupe-kingdom|Nupe]].
hausa-kingdoms.r: Each kingdom was ruled by a sarki with a council of titled officials, drawing revenue from markets, crafts and tribute. The states never formed a single empire: they fought one another, paid tribute at times to the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]], the [[s:songhai-empire|Songhai Empire]] or [[s:kwararafa|Kwararafa]], and shared a common language and trade network. [[e:islam|Islam]] spread among rulers and merchants from the 14th century, alongside older [[e:hausa|Hausa]] beliefs.
hausa-kingdoms.e: Between 1804 and 1808 the [[e:jihad|jihad]] of [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio]] overthrew most of the [[e:hausa|Hausa]] dynasties and replaced them with Fulani-led [[e:emirate|emirates]] of the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]]. Some Hausa royal lines survived in exile, at Abuja, [[s:sultanate-of-maradi|Maradi]] and [[s:sultanate-of-tsibiri|Tsibiri]]. The emirates passed under British rule in 1903.
hausa-kingdoms.re: Sunni Islam and Hausa traditional religion

hanseatic-league.t: The league of north German merchant towns that dominated trade across the Baltic and North Sea from the 13th to the 16th century.
hanseatic-league.o: German merchant associations trading in the Baltic grew up in the 12th and 13th centuries, led by [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]]. Towns such as [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]], Danzig and Riga cooperated to protect their merchants abroad. The first general diet (Hansetag) met in [[e:lubeck|Lübeck]] in 1356, usually taken as the point when the merchants' Hanse became a league of towns.
hanseatic-league.r: The Hansa had no constitution, standing army or common treasury; up to some 200 towns at its height sent envoys to diets that coordinated trade policy and boycotts. Its four great overseas offices (Kontore) were in [[e:london|London]], Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod. Cogs carried grain, [[e:timber|timber]], [[e:fur-trade|furs]], wax, fish and cloth. The Peace of Stralsund of 1370, after war with [[e:denmark|Denmark]], marked its peak.
hanseatic-league.e: Stronger territorial states, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English competition and the shift of trade to the Atlantic eroded the Hansa in the 16th century, and the last diet met in 1669. [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]], [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] and [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]] kept the Hanseatic name; the Free and Hanseatic City of [[e:hamburg|Hamburg]] and the Free Hanseatic City of [[e:bremen|Bremen]] remain city-states today.
